LADIES LETTER.
MY DEAR NELLIE,

A blouse for indoor wear which I had shown to me the other day was of satin with it fancy front. It had a pointed embroidered plastron in front over a ohemisette of guipure lace lined with white satin. The embroidery is cartied out in jet and chenille on white kid, and a row of black and white silk fringe edges it all round. The points reach the waist back and front. On this blouse the sleeves ate satin to midway between the shoulder and elbow, embroidery the rest of the way, ending in a pointed piece of guipure fall- ing over the hand.

I have recently seen some charming fkocks anti coats for children and young girls. A quaint little dress of Tintoretto bin& was made in a delicate Jihad° of rose-pink, with a row of embroidery in pink and white silk round the bottom of the skirt. Round the shoulders there was a draped fichu of gauze, with a gathered frill at the edge. There was a dress of green velveteen, with a plain skirt, and a blouse bodice and gauged sleeves of soft silk of a lighter shade of green. There were soft frills of silk at the wrists, and also on the front of the bodice, forming a kind of full jabot. This model would look well in many shades of velveteen, such as fraise or dragon's. blood among the warm colourings, or sapphire or cerulean among the blues. There was a pretty dress of sky-blue velveteen, with a vest of finely tucked'black silk, and a folded band of the same.

The most modish millliaery has a thucti of lace about it, which reminds me that a lace scarf is an indispensable finish to the outdoor attire of che moment, but do not tie it in a bow unless you would write yourself down benightedly provincial. Twine the scarf round the neck, and let the ends bang down in front inside your coat. Toques are being much exploited now of pheasant and part- ridge feathers. These are handsome and modish, but though becoming to a really clear complexion, they are not generally so. Sttings have not caught on so much as was expected utter all. The im- mensely high collar worn on nearly all the dressy coats accounts largely for their ahanionment, the combination of strings and collar giving too bunched-up an appearance, besides ieeling smothery. Though in many respects a vast im• provement on recent seasous' niiilieery, he prent; still retains a good deal of the airy inoonsmiv.aca which has been so marked the last few season; of the end of the century. Two examples recently seen at smart millinery ataliers occur to me: one, a transparent white tulle shape, dotted entirely over with ermine tails and trimmed Nrith chrysanthe- mums; another of ermine, entirely trimmed with a profusion of roses Ind big wiiite feathers.

Among the autumn novelties are dresses in cloth of velveteen, bordered round the edge with a band of white kid, edged with brown fur. A green cloth 'gown finished in this way looked very well with a narrow bordEr of beaver at the edge. Another, in brown velveteen, has a similar trimming, and a third, made of brown cloth, is finished in the same way. Fur ie LlEeci in narrow lines on skirts, as it was some seasons since, in combination with fancy braid, embroidery, or peseementerie. It is a we...4°Ni way of using fur, especially when the skirts are worn so foolishly long as they are at present. Large feather fans are once again being worn, though the small cues predominate. The black eagle'e feather is considered very chic, From frame come most dainty little ventails, with ex- quisitely painted views of fevouzito resorts in one eorner on chicken skin. Tha rest of the fan is :levered with eparkling paillettee in banks of celour, and the handles are tied with a bunch of the favourite flower of the place. The hair continues to be dreseed high, but it must present a neat appearance, end is no longer frizzed out all round. It is si4 4tJy ondui6, and a pretty ornament such as a heiech of flowers, a fillet of tulle or ribinen, or an oetrich tip is worn in the centre. Jewels are wo• aby those who possess them, to toe exclusiom nf other additions, but these favoured folk are in the minority. silk is still the chief material for children's frocks for partiec. Aecordeon-pleated or plainly gathered skires are set into yokes of lace or paffed muslin, or made of bengelino closely tucked or stitched. Knots of satin ribben make a dainty finish. The sleeves are almost al waya long enough to roach the elbows. As little girls get very hot in dancing, some mothers prefer that they should have their party frocks cut away about the neck, as when the throat is overheated and much encumbered with collar, ribbon, lace, etectera, there is con- siderable risk of chill when the little creatures leave the hot rooms fur home.

Apropos of new muffs, many are made of sable lined with ermine, or with delicated tinted, or white satin. Others are of ermine lined with satin, and trimmed with sprays of lace held by a bouquet of violets. Even the ordinary regulation fur muffs have in many cases yielded to the soft fascinations of lace, coming in full frills from the inside to hang gracefully. Your loving

Except in a cd.rriageonuffs are little worn. The reasm for this is that we are all too athletic nowadays to patronise such a hand-confining article. We want our hands to use, not to coddle 'in in a bundle of fur and lace. The bicycle has doubtless done much towards banishing ths muff. We learnt, when we took sip this pastime that a pair of stout gloves meets all our require- ments in the way of warmth, and that the muff, when taking exercise is both unhealthy and cumbersome. It is jut four hundred 'years since the muff mado Its appearance in Europe, net in Russia as one miLzlat sup- pose, but iu V,nic.e. The Venetians were great lovers of costly furs, and by a process of evolution, probably muffs grew out of the voluminous sleeves, senators and other roverenit persons used to wear.

div.head: "WOMEN'S CHAT."
div.p: "WOMEN'S CHAT."

The decision of the Queen to viait Bordighera fleet spring,has caused the ereatest setiefactioa in Iraiy. The Augst Hotel, the new east wing of which is laring pre- pared for Her Majesty's receptien, is magnificently situated, eemmanding the finest view it is possible to get of the Riviera.. It is a handsome hetel, and arranged somewhat in the Italian style, with parquet flooring,t instead of carpets, and light cane furniture. Tao firs, impression is a little cold, but there is the Italian sky and the Italian 611:1 te glee werinsh and color. 'Ttie Empress Frederick spent three twentise of the year in the same spot, wad it is probably due to her very favourable account of the place that the Qiieen ha z selected it fvr her forthcoming Continental holdisjae. The selection of Christmes presents is occupying much of the Queen's time just neve, and her private apartments resemble nothing mote titan a linen magni- ficent bazaar. Each gift is carefully selected and th7,ught out, nothing is decided upon in a hurry. Numerous consignments of mechanical toys too have been des• patched to Windsor, and many a hearty laugh has the Sovereign indulged in ever especially good ideas. It is invariably observed that Her Majesty takes the greatest interest in this branch of the selection, naming each child the toy is intended for as it is selected and set aside.

Once upon a time we were contented that our Christ- mas padding should be prepared in the usual and national manner, arid stuffed only with things one stood a fair chance of dieesting. Nowadays however we have altered all that. This year the "feetivo" pudding, to be up-to-date, must contain rings, brooches, scarf-pins sovereigns and half soveeigns. thimbles, buttons, etc. When some well-known society foles have inadvertently swallowed a few surprises of this sort, it will probably dawn upon people that the old-fashioned Christmas pud- ding was a better idea after all. The usual Christmas appeals seem likely to suffer from the many demands made upon the charitably &sensed, en account of the Patriotic and other Funds in con- nection with the war. Many institutions are already complaining of a falling off in their subscriptions, and similar complaints are also coming from the clergy, and others, whe, at tbis time of the year, organize their own little benefits and distributions. It has all along been feared that the War Funds would cause some shrinkage in the normal flow of charity this winter, though of course the exceptional demands occasioned by the war, ought really to be met by exceptional generoiity. There should be less doubt about this owing to the general prosperity of the country, and for this reason it is to b 3 hoped that the sick and needy at home will not be less cared for than usual during the coming festive season. In the pretty story which has been published of the bedridden blind man at Bristol, who insisted upon being propped by the window in order that he might " see" Her Majesty as she psesed, some people will find a sus- picious resemblance to a hull, but those who have had experienco of the blind know differently. One one occa- sion the Duke of Westminster was visiting the Royal College for the Blind at Norwood, and was admiring the beautiful prospect from deo College grounds. " What a pity it is " he remarked to Dr. Campbell. the blind Principal of the Institution, " that your pupils are unable to see this lovely view." "Ah '' replied Dr. Campbell, referring to the vivid imagination of the " we can see such beauties in this scene, as your Grace never even dreamed of." On this subjeet it has often been said by intelligent blind people, that it is in the power of the sighted to render a very real service to the blind by describing to them the objects which are before them at the moment, the imagination of the blind enabling them to picture the scone of which the outline has been-described.

One is glad to see that the governors nf the Middlesex Hospital are occupied with a scheme for the thorough investigation of cancer, and have decided to devote £6EO a year to the purposes of research. That there is a cure for cancer we have no doubt, and in all probability it will be found within the present generation, if rot within the next ten years. Possibly it may be di covered by chance, as the efficacy of quinine is said to have been discovered, possibly by faith in what is :alle.d the wisdom of nature,which enabled a medical m3n to find salicine in the marshiy districts where aheumatism most abounded, but the stronger probability is,that the cure for cancer will be discovered by means of pains— taking and elaborate research, such as that which the governors of the hospital referred to intend to promote. Meanwhile if SOPISO millionaire had sufficient enli.7hten- meet to offer a reward of £25,000 for the discovery of a cure, which would satisfy the Royal College oi Physicians, he might in that case tw,sten the solution of the problem, and hand down his name to posterity as a benefactor of roankine.

'Welt dear, if you will, feu will, but. for Heavez's sake =eke baste. Who knows where Mr., rieauwerth is He may be out with Bob, awl wlia can you do? You may even meet Mr. Felton again." Bully did net totes to more words; she seized the key and ran to the head of the stairs. Quite lately she had gone down these stairs laughing and happy, now she felt as if she should go mad. She must get help from Alec. Oh, he had known it, and he had tried to warn her and she had not understood. She ran down the narrow stairs and reached the passage opposite the garden door. What should she do? She did not knew whore Alec wa's to be found, but if she could see Bob he would be kind and would help her. Even Bob appeared like a preserver. As she stood in the passage she listened and then the blood rushed to her cheeks, for she distinctly heard voices in the old library. It was James's voice, and every now and then he laughed—a low, horrid laugh—as if he were much amused. The interview had only mad' him laugh when it had made her feel utterly wretated. He had kissed her cheeks, and they still felt burning from shame and anger. She trembled now for fear he might come out again and find her here. She moved on tip-toe and approached the outer door. She tried to lift the latch very slowly with- out making a noise. She succeeded, but dared not shut it, so, closing it, she hurried on to the stables. At all events, the Feltons were behind her; she need not fear meeting them. The moon was rising and shedding a dim, misty light around. Her father had not yet returned home, for the carriage had not come in. She then took courage to call Bob. There was no answer. Bob All was silent. She looked back at the house. She knew that Alec had the best room given to him, for he had told her so, but there was no light in it now. No hope that she could make Alec hear. She did not dare call him, but once again she called Bob.
"Is that Miss Ruby ? " said a voice. Then Ruby heard a scramble down the old ivy-covered tree which stood near the house, and Bob came gliding down. _

"There ain't no one with you, is there, Miss Ruby? Don't tell on me." "0 Bob, I want you. Where is Mr. Beauworth ? I want him very much for I am in trouble." "My shakes! Where's Mr. Alec? that's what I want to know. He said he was going to saunter round, and that he would be in soon. He said he wanted to think. It takes him a long time to think," and Bob chuckled. "0 Bob, you like him, don't you ? " "Well, I expect I does, Miss Ruby, or I shouldn't be here."

"He is kind and will help me ;find him for me." "He'll be wanting help hisself I shouldn't wonder, but I'm keeping an eye on him." Ruby did not heed all Bob's talk. She was thinking how she could see Alec. "I must see him, Bob. Find him for me." "Have you been sent by anyone, Miss Ruby, because you might be a bait—a sort of a little thing they put an a hook for to catch the fish they want to gobble up." "Sent? Oh, no, Bob, no one knows lam here; and I'll do anything for you if you will find him." "The squire wouldn't like it, Miss Ruby." , "Oh, you are all afraid of papa." "He don't let anyone go against him, that's the truth," grinned Bob. "He's always been so kind to me till to-day. Bob, find Mr. Beauworth for me." "I'll go and look round for him, but where will you be, Miss Ruby ? " This was a difficulty. Ruby felt that she must make haste before her father came home. She had been so much accustomed to exact obedience that now her conscience reproached her. "I'll slip in the coach-house, Bob; only make haste."
Bob thought a moment, then he said: "Ths.t won't do, Miss Ruby. The squire might come and there would be a noise. Run up the ladder into the loft."
•Haley bad often run up Quire toinenoe herself or to find her kittens. She did not hesitate.

She sat 4-4;-wit on a truss of hay an.d waited, her heart beating hard. What should aka tell Alec when he came? How could she explain her sudden horror at James Felton's conduot ? The rude announced:a:o that she was to be his sweoli,art, and they were to be married directly. Ohl how could she tell him all that?

Ten minutes went by, then suddenly she heard voices, and to her horror she saw her father return- ing from his drive. She dared not be seen by him; it was the first time she had hidden herself from him. Then Bob came running up to her father, exclaiming wildly: ' "It's the horses, sir, at the lower meadow as has gone out into the road." Martin, the old coachman, suggested to his master he should take the trap and go and turn them back. - -

"Oh, I had better come with you, Martin," muttered the squire. "You would be all night driving them in. If we drive round the park and out by the lower gate we can head them, but who can have let them out ? "
"Perhaps it's young Mr. Felton," suggested Bob.

The squire turned the horse's head and drove away. He was out of sight in a minute and Bob ran up the ladder. "He's coming, Miss Ruby; you will have, to be quick." "0 'Bob, how did the horses--" "Very easily, Miss Ruby. Someone must have opened the gate." But at this minute Alec himself came hurrying up the ladder. "Ruby," he said, taking her hand, "dear Ruby, you should not be here." "I must tell you. Oh, you knew it this
morning ? " "That you are to—be engaged to James Felton? Yes."
"Alec, save me! save me! I can't be his wife, I hate him. You said that--" _ _ _ _

"Hush! "Ruby, don't repeat it. I would help you if I could, but your father--" "He does not understand. He tlinks I could love anyone, but I hate Mr. Felton. I have no one to ask but you. Tell me what I must do? " "Why are you so unhappy over it? Your father says that you will obey him. What can Ido for you? " "He would not have let James Felton speak so if-"

"Yes, it is true, Ruby. Your father means you to marry this man." ; "Tell me what to do ? " The girl took hold of his hand, and Alec felt that he was standing on the edge of a precipice. He lovod this girl, and would save her if he could, but he had been trusted. It went against his Principles to do anything which might be thought dishonourable.
"Ruby, dear Ruby, how can I advise you. I know nothing against your Australian cousin. Your father told me--"

"But I will not marry him. lam too young, and Ido not love him. 0, Cousin Alec, I will not do it. Help me! You said that you would if I wanted help." "Then I will, Ruby. I should be a coward if I refused this help. But there is only one way." "Tell me ; I will do anything--" "Ruby, do you remember that this morning we played it eing,,married--" Ruby turned her face away. "Oh, forgive me, I was a child and I did not understand, but now I see it was a foolish game. . .

"Yes, it was a foolish game; but, Ruby, I am goinr, to play it in earnest." Ru*by turned her head away. "Will you be my wife? I will love you and take care of you and---" "No, no; you only say that because you want to help me. I did not mean that. I know now that one cannot play at things like that." "It isn't play, darling. I loved you the first minute I saw you, but I would never have said so unless yoa had come to me of your own free will." "Oh, it is not true. You are only sayinc, this because you are so good and you want to help Only tell me what to do." Ruby seemed to him at this minute a perfect woman.

"I must win your love, but I want to save you." Ruby puti her hand 'in his as a trusting child might have done, and all Alec's chivalry was awakened. He felt now that he would go through fire and water to save her.

"Cou3in Alec, I do love you, and you may do what you like, but I 'don't -want you to do any- thing from pity. I am really afraid of that man. Save me from him." "Then, darling, will you be my wife?" "I will tell papa that I will marry you but not James," said Ruby, blushing like a peony." "No, dearest," he said, taking her small hand in his. "No, you must say nothing; except that you will no marry James Felton. Then I will boldly ask your father if I may try to win you. 0 Ruby, 3tou do not. understand that a man's greatest ,hanni-

ness is to to loved and to love a ~ilia.ll. 'the you. Any suffering is worth that." "But you must have loved someone else," laid Ruby, the young heart suddenly feeling the pangs of jealousy. "I loved my adopted mother. I have never loved another woman till I saw you." "Then I will be your wife if you will have me," and a smile parted Ruby's lips. "But, of course, I must tell papa." "I am afraid that if you do-" "I will do what you tell me," she said, sud- denly remembering that she must not think only of happiness. "I cannot tell you to be untrue, dearest, but wait a little while."

"When papa comes back I will tell him that I will never marry James Felton." "Yes, and before I go away 1 will tell him that I will wait for you as long as you like. In the meantime promise me one thing, Ruby, do not let James tease you, and do not ever speak to him alone. He might annoy you, for lam sure he wants very much to make you his wife." At this moment there was a whistle heard.

"That is Bob's signal. He told me that I should hear it when you must go back." "Oh, did you tell Bob? Is he to be trusted ? " "I know nothing about him except that he has done me a great service. I cannot explain it to you, but I feel sure that he will do anything for a person he is fond of." , Alec would not take advantage of his position, even though Ruby had said so much, but he raised her hand to his lips. Ruby felt how much the two men differed. She made no resistance now, and Alec felt that for some unexplainable purpose she had been brought up in ignorance. "Ruby, we must go. Can you get back ? " "Yes, I came by the garden door. I made Nancy give me the key." "I will see you back." "Oh, no, don't, don't, Alec; he is there—he might see you. I feel as if he would do you some harm if he saw you with me." "Most likely; but I am able to dare him to do his worst so that he spares you. When we meet, Ruby, you must say nothing about this." Another soft whistle and the two, made lovers in such a strange way, separated hastily. Ruby ran lightly down the ladder, and found Bob at the bottom. _
"Go home now, Miss Ruby; the squire is coming back. Someone must have met the horses and turned them in."

Ruby ran back to the house, and Alec, who would not follow her, saw her shut the door. Bob joined him at this moment. "Have. you been making love to Miss Ruby ? " said Bob. It was better to trust Bob all in all.

"Yes, Bob. She has just told me that James Felton has been persecuting her, and that her father wishes to marry her to him." "Ods Daggs!" exclaimed Bob, "then that's their game; but what did they want you for? Can't make head nor tail of it." _
"I am wanted to make things easy; but it was Miss Ruby who objected—l would not have inter- fered otherwise." __ . _
"You had best get out of the way, Mr. Alec. Keep an eye on the young 'nn; there is no chance of his loving you over much." When the squire returned he found Bob waiting for him.
"Is the horses safe, sir? " "Yes; I wish I knew who let them out. Ilelp Martin, Bob, and then come indoors; I can't have you making noises in the night. I shall come out late and smoke."

Bob touched his cap. "Where be I to sleep, sir? " "There's a bed in the old passage-room. Now that the rooms are opened, you may as well use them. By the way, come with me, Bob; I want to give you some instructions." The squire led the way into the lower passage, first going through the hall. A few minutes earlier he would have met Ruby creeping up the little stairs. But now there was only the light streaming from the door of the library, where the two Feltons were still in earnest , conversation. The squire paused and listened for a moment ; then, as if ashamed of being s?e,n eavesdropping, he re- marked to Bob:

"The gentlemen are busy, and won't like to be disturbed; but if you sleep in this little room, Bob, you can be handy for anything they want." "Yes, sir," said Bob, feeling delighted. To be in reach of his enemies was what he wanted. But if they were all tarred with the same brush, why was the squire wanting to have a spy over the other two? Bob turned this over in his mind. He was feeling that he could not be even with the devil—this was pride that was to have a fall. "Look here, Bob, there is a door at the top of the staircase which Nancy has orders always to keep shut." _ _ _

"Then she don't obey orders," thought Bob, chuckling. "I don't want anyone to be able to go up here to disturb Miss Ruby. She is not accustomed to strangers, and if she heard noises, she might-- In fact, Bob, you are to allow no one to go up there. Do you understand ? " "Yes, sir. No one ain't to go up there and to open the little door, and if they do-" "Then come and tell me at once. Bring your shake-down here to-night, and you won't be dis- turbing anyone if you do scream." Bob looked humble and stupid, so that the squire repeated: "You are to let no one come down here. Do you understan,d, Bob ? " "Yes, sir; nor go up? ' "I meant that, of course. That is settled; you can go now." He walked on to the library, and Bob was making his way back, when he thought better of it, and stopped to listen. His ideas of honour were not acute, especially as he had to deal with the three men who were, as he knew, anxious to do what Bob determined should not be done if he could help it. However, he could hear nothing but quick conversation; so turning away, he hurried off to fetch his shake-down and to help the old butler.

"Bnt I'll be even with 'em," he repeated, to himself. "The devil ain't so sly as I am." An hour later no one was in the ball but Sir Harry and his daughter. The great logs were heaped on the hearth, the flames leaped up, illumin- ating the old wood-work with fitful lights; but all these tokens spoke of an English home and of English love. Sir Harry, with knitted brows, was standing by the carved mantelpiece, and near him stood Ruby. clasping his arm. "I always thought that you would obey me, Ruby." "Papa, you never spoke to me first; you never told me—but you sent him." "If he was wanting in courtesy, I will speak to him."

"You said that I was a child, papa. lam too young to marry." "What nonsense! I must be a judge of your happiness. Have I not been a kind father to you? Tell me, Ruby ? " "You have always been good; but, papa, I can't explain, only I can never see him again." "Ruby, for my sake, don't speak like that. I have tried to do my duty by you; I have tried to keep you from harm---" It seemed more as if he were speaking to himself and not to her.

"I will stay with you, papa, always." "Years ago James Felton did me a great service, and I then told him that I would do what I could to repay him. He asked me for the hand of--for your hand, Ruby, for his son, and I promised. I can not now say no, Ruby." "No, but I can, papa—surely I can," cried Ruby. "It would be of no use, child. If I could have spared you, I would." "Is that why you never told me ? " said Ruby, sinking down on the hearthrug. "Yes, I did hope—but now—" "I see, you cannot break your word. A Beau- worth never does, but your promise does not bind me, papa." "Yes, it does, Ruby; for my sake, you must become James Felton's wife."

'What does it all mean? To go away with him, and to leave you and Cousin Alec, who has been so kind to me? Oh, I cannot; do not ask me to do such a thing, papa." "James will be here in a minute, Ruby. For my sake, do not refuse." "Papa!" The girl's face expressed such a horror that Sir Harry was startled. He had never before seen Ruby look like that. Ruby thought of Alec. Perhaps he would come, and all would be right. He had said that he would save her. He must save her. "Papa, will you ask him—no--tell him that I cannot—that I never shall love him. Won't you tell him that? Sir Harry thought a minute, and then he answered: "Go to your room, Ruby, and I will do what I can for you ; but remember that if James claim° 37011. I must keen my word."

- "Must! 0 papa, can't you cto as you tale ? " "Go to Nancy, Ruby, now, and I will come to you." Sir Harry turned to the window, and with one despairing gli,nne at him, Ruby hurried away. Left alone, Sir Harty sat down and tried to think out a plan. What should he do? How multi he, save her He could not blame the Feltons. ffè looked back, and knew that he had long ago made his bed, and that he must not complain about lying on it now. But could he do anything to save the girl he loved? If he would give her up, but he will not give up the estate, and without her he cannot have it.. How can I blame him? How could I guess that this child-"

There were sounds outside, and Sir Harry strai;litened himself. "Well, Sir Harry, that little bird of yours is not the meek dove you once told us she was. I think that you have spoilt her. The governor and I said so long ago." "She is not the girl for you, James. Listen. Is there no other way? What can I give you instead of her? " "Great Scot! That is a new tune. When we are touching the goal, you ask us to turn back! It isn't from scruples; they don't sprout in your soil, at all events, said the elder Felton.
"You shall have the estate, but spare the child. She is not the child I took her for. It is the fault of--"
"Of course, it is your fault. Your id.,s was too foolish. You wanted Beauworth to make that will

"I was wrong." "But that don't matter. A week is ample for us. You are sure that those papers make every- thing square? As for Miss Ruby, a little discipline won't hurt her. She had better learn to obey." "You shall not-"

"Come, we are going to have some supper." "Is he coming ? " asked the squire, without look- ing at his cousins. "Dun't bother about him. quarter, at least." "We shall have to go to Rabbitts's to-night to send off various telegrams," said the elder Felton. "Will you come, squire? No, it would be better that you should not appear." At eight o'clock the supper was brought in. The old butler asked if Mr. Beauworth was coming in, and James Felton answered that he had gone away or the night. Where was he?
Carte blanche in that
(To be continued.)

div.head: NOBLER THAN REVENGE.
div.p: NOBLER THAN REVENGE.
By ESME STUART, Author of "In the Dark," "Inscrutable,' "A Woman of Forty," "Sara's Mother," Brc.

" SYNOPSIS OF PRECEDING CHAPTERS: On his way to visit his cousin, Sir Harry Beauworth, Alec Beauworth, heir to the title, is set upon by two men and knocked senseless. Sir Harry Beauworth has a bad reputation. Bob Rabbitts, son of the evil-look- ing landlord of the Dog and Duck, revives Alec, and determines, as he has the chance, to enter Sir Harry's service for a time to see that Alec comes to no harm. Sir Harry has one daughter, Ruby, a beautiful and unsophisticated girl, who has never been allowed to see the world, and whom her father intends to marry to an Australian, James Felton, who with his father, Tom Felton, appears to have a powerful influence over him. These Feltons are the men who tried to kill Alec, though he never saw their faces, and it is obvious that they acted at the Instigation of the baronet, who has some secret reason for wishing to be rid of the heir. Alec, when he sees Ruby, falls in love with her, and not knowing his danger determines, if possible, to stay and win her. Though he has no intention of allow- .ing Ruby to marry Alec, Sir Harry Beauworth plays upon Alec's affections in order to induce him to make a will in Ruby's favour. Alec consents, and thereafter his destruction is practically decided upon by Sir Harry and the Feltons, so as to pave the way for a division of all the money and the estates which, in the ordinary course, would have fallen to Alec.

div.head: CHAPTER Xl.
div.p: CHAPTER Xl.

It was getting quite dark, and upstairs in Ruby's room the curtains were drawn across the windows. Nancy was preparing tea, but the young girl was sitting in an arm-chair with her head hidden on her arm. As Nancy moved about she tried to cheer Ruby, who seemed suddenly to have left girlhood behind her.
"Tain't so bad," said Nancy, "when you are accustomed to them, dear. He's well grown, and he's got all his senses, and that is something to be thankful for."

"This morning I was so happy, and now - 0 Nancy, I felt so frightened when he came near me and tried to kiss me, and when I wouldn't let him touch me he laughed and said: "There's time for that when we are married."
"So there is, dearie. And it's your father's wish."

"That's the worst part of it. I asked papa to let me remain with him always and not to let me marry anyone, and he only said that he had promised." "Well, it's the way of some fathers, and the squire don't allow no contradiction." "But father loves me, and I saw that he was suffering." "Then, dear, be sure he can't help himself." "If he can't help himself I shall help him. I won't marry that horrid man. I thought this morning that I did not mind him, but now I know, oh, I know, that he is cruel and wicked." "Your father knows best."

Ruby started up. "0 Nancy, the Beauworths are brave. In those letters of papa's, written to his mother, he said if she called him brave it was because he was a Beauworth. I will be brave, too." "Hush, dear! I think now that your father always meant to give you to this young gentleman, for he told us never to let you see a man or to talk to a stranger. Most likely he didn't want you to take a fancy to another." "I think that my cousin Alec must know about It. This morning I was such a child, and he will think-"

"Poor child, poor child," said Nancy, as if to herself; "you're over young for such a thing." "Nancy, dear, children don't marry, do they? I must tell you, I feel so afraid of Cousin James. I shall never be happy alone with him as I am with Cousin Alec; he is so kind and so good to me. Nancy, speak to father and tell him that I will do all he likes but not that. Only last week I should not have minded so nj.uch, but now, oh, I cannot do it, Nancy. Must one be dreadfully afraid of one's husband ? "

"Men aren't worth much any of them, but it's not for me to say nothing. Your father would be angry with me. Mr. Felton ain't like Cother nice young gentleman, that's certain sure, but, my dear, a man is a man, and you must make the best of hip, and that's the long and short of it." "Oh, I can't, I can't, Nancy; he frightens me so much. I think it must mean that Cousin Alec knew it, because he said that if I wanted a friend I was to ask him."

"Come. come, dearie, don't take on so. Your father will be angry. You must just tell him, clearie, and see what he says, but it's my belief that you had better make the best of it. You'll get accustomed to him in time." "But Ccusin Alec said that one ought to love one's husband, and I don't love that man, and I never shall. This morning I was a child, and now I feel as if I were a hundred years old." "It all comes of your bringing up. The gentle- men will soon be coming in. The squire said that he had to go to the town to see a lawyer." "I will go and see if 1 can find Mr. Beauworth, Nancy." "No, dear, it is as much as my place is worth to let you. You mustn't go." "But, Nancy, I will go; I am not a child any longer. If it's father's will, as that man said it was, then father can't think me a child. Quick, Nancy, where is the key of the stairs ? " "I dursn't give it to you." Ruby was not listening. She seemed suddenly transformed from an unthinking child to a woman with a will. The scene with James had stirred depths of which she had before been ignorant, and she now saw clearly that Alec had that morning tried to prepare her for what was coming. He was good and brave. She would appeal to him in case, as James had said, her father would not listen to her entreaties. Many little scenes now came back to her mind when her father's will had been law. She felt as if she were drowning, and that she must cling to something. Alec had, indeed, done his work well, for she thought only of him. Without heeding Nancy, she ran to the passage door through which James had gone out, after he had told her in no very gentle tones, on her refusal to kiss him, that it was her father's wish, and that she must make up her mind to accept him as a lover. She reached the big door and pushed it. It was locked! Never had this happened before in the daytime. "So lam really a prisoner," she exclaimed, stamping her foot. "Did that man dare to lock me in?"

No ene would now have recognised the gentle Ruby had they seen her at this moment. But she felt desperate. The squire had not reckoned with that instinct of purity and self-preservation which is often found in the most unsophisticated natures. Ruby ran back to her room, her large hazel eyes flashing with new resolve. She was a woman now—a woman of action.

"Nancy, give me the key at once! They have locked that big door. Did you know it?" "Come, come, dear, you are all excited; you must be quiet. You will make yourself ill. Come, sit down quiet." "I won't, Nancy! Did father tell you anything when he came here just before Mr. Felton ? "
"Well, dear, I won't deny but that the squire did come, and, ' Nancy, ' says he, Miss Ruby is to stay in this afternoon, Mr. James is wanting to see ben ' "
"He thinks, perhaps, that James is nice. 0 Nancy, you don't know how he- Oh, I can't talk about it. You should not have left us alone."

"I was only in the next room. I heard him talking, and then I heard you call out and came running in to see him lauahing at you." "Don't talk any more, Nancy. Give me the key." "I dursn't, dear, the squire don't let us disobey him. You know it, child. We are all mortal afraid of him. There ain't a man, woman, or child, that does not fear him, and that is the truth. Don't ask me for the key. What do you want to do ? "
"I will have it, Nancy. I will tell papa that I ordered you to give it to me."
Ruby an out-to the passage where Nancy usually kept the key on a hobk behind the door. It was not there.
"Nancy, where is it? I will have it!" Never had Nancy seen her charge like this. . _

"It's in my poC.ket. The squire said that you was not to go out till he came to fetch you." "Papa does not understand. Give it to me, Nancy." "I shall lose my place," wailed Nancy, "and my poor girl, who is a widow and lives rent free because lam here, depend on it, the squire will turn her out. He said he would if I ever dis- obeyed him. Have pity on me, Miss Ruby." "Give me the key, Nancy, I must have it." Nemcv took it out of her Docket.

div.head: AWAY UP IN THE AIR.
div.p: AWAY UP IN THE AIR.
In America they have recently been erecting business. buildings from fifteen to twenty-four etories high ; and the np.e floors rent for almost or quite as much as the lower ones.

The possilllity of this is of 'course due to the develop— ment of the lift, or I' elevator," as our cousins over there name it. I personally know of one of these tall tuildinge, in the twenty-third story of which there i 3 a fine and flourishing restaurant. I dined up there one summer day last year, and might have tossed a loaf of bzead down on the weather vane of the highest churth ste.-ple in the city. But there ! 14 is the lifting machine that does it. Any arrangement that takes us off the earth, without puting us te treubie and exertion, opens a Eew era of existence. Do you imagine I should have eaten a. clvpsn the twenty-third story of that Tower of Babel if t•i!,d been obliged te climb twenty-two long fligk.ts of stairs to get there ?

Scar csly ;for of all the various ways of making a man's legs ache, and taking the breath out of him, climbing stairs beats tbe band. There is no better test of elasticity and toughn: al of the muscles, and of the con- ditions of one's heart and breathing apparatus. All of which brings me round to the spct I ought perhaps to bavo started trona—Mrs. Turner and her troubles. She says that for ten years or nacre she was bothered with indigestion—or dyspepsia, if you care to all it that ;it is exactly th 3 same thing. The luxury of a good appetite was to her only a dim and fading memory ; the ate as a tired and sleepy sentry walks— only because she had to.
And even then she as punished for it; for after she had taken (most carefully did she select it) a meal of victuals, she was ture to suffer from pain and misery at the stomach, chest, and sides.

l• My breathing," she says, " alarmed and worried Lai quite as much as any of the other symptoms of my complaint. Sometimes it almost seemed as if my breath were going altogether out of my body. 55 a bird flies out ot a cage when the door is left open. I gct about on the level fairly well, hut when I triad to climb stairs I had to stop and gasp on every step. The effort would Fct my heart jumping end beating ; and I caught mouthfuls of air 38 you have seen children clutch attita of down floating through a room. " In hope of ralief I tried one kind of medicine after another, but for yesrs I never had the good Lrtune to find the right one. I was very, very vreak. and did my wok only in the half-way fashion that people must do it in who have tbe will without the power. " At length I chanced to read in a newspaper about how persons troubled with the same ailment had been ontimly cured by Mother Seigel's syrup after having suffered at much and as long as Iliad. I began taking it, and the first bottle did me so much good I felt ocnvinceci it would help me out. I continued using the syrup, and in a little time it did for me what the paper said it had done for 90 many other afflicted ones.

"I becAme able to eat and digest, and my breathing got to Le as free and easy as when I had no disease to depress and half suffocate me. I could go upstairs quickly and lightly as a girl. I slept well and gained strength with every dose of this wonderful remedy. I am now in excellent health and give all the credit to Mother Seid,el's Syrup."— Mary Turner, Ragg Cottage, Alawere, South Molton, March 17, 1899.

" Five years," writes another, " I went through the wretchedness of indigestion. I had pain at the chest and all the other symptoms and conse- quences of that common and dreadful complaint. Nmhing did me any good until I began using Mother Seigei's Syrup. This speedily cured me, and I have never had the trouble since. I know of nothing that is so sure and quick in breaking up a cold as the Syrup."—Charlotte Suodin, 52,Hunter-street,Nortkamp ton, January 24, 1899. It is all of a pisce. • The members. of the Warrington Draughts Club have taken a step in the right direction to induce their players to turn up to practice. A handicap has been started among the members, each player being handicapped according to his ability. This gives the worst player in the club an equal chance with the best of securing the first prize. No doubt now the ball has b.-ten set in motion, other clubs in the town will not be slow to recognise the benefits which must accrue from a handicap of this descrip- tion. •We may mention that the scale adopted is that by Mr. J Toner, particulars of which may be found in Sturges' Guide page 29, and also .in Dunne's Guide and Companion.

The unfinished heat in the second round of the Liverpool Championship between Messrs. Cain and Jones ended in favour of Cain by 2 games to nil and 3 draws. Cain then met Morrall in the third round, and the result of the first sitting of Satur- day last was one win to Morrall and two games drawn. At the sitting on Monday Cain scored the firt game played, and the next ended in a draw. In the following game Morrall was called to time, and failing to make his move before the expiration of another minute his opponent was awarded the game, the hat ending—Cain 2, Morrell 1, drawn 3. -Cain and Nixon have now to play off in the final.

The small diagram will enable our readers to understand the notation by which the 'moves of the game are recorded. slack occupies the squares num- bered 1 to 12 and white those numbered 21 to 32. The figures thus 11-15 indicate that a move is made from and to the squares so numbired.Black has the opening move and the rairs of fignres apply alternately to Black and White to the close. '

The monthly meeting of the Warringten Town Council was held on Tues ley evenine, the Mayor (Alderman Henry Roberts) preeiding. Thera were preeent the Deputy-Mayor (Anierman J E Wright), Aliermen W Bolton, J Faircloue,h, R W Francomb,T H Sutton. Coun- cillors, J Baird, A Bennett, T Burton, J Crosfield. D S Duncan, James Evans. John Evans, L Ellison, L Green- ine,J S Green,l Jolley,A J Jolley,John Lee,F W Monks, A Peacock. W Pierpeint G Plumpton, J Roberts, F R Robert, W Roger', J Shillcock, J Smethurst, D Tinnion, with Messrs. J L Whittle (Town Clerl),S Wilson (Deputy Town Clerk),J Fairhurst (Borough Treasurer), f Longdin (Borough Surveyor),J H Gornall (Medical Officer),J Deas (Water Engineer), and W S Haddock (Gas Engineer). Watch Committee.—The Reservist Policemen. At a meeting of the above'committee it was resolved that the I &lowing members be appointed a sub-com- mtttee to assist the Chief Constable in carrying otet the duties of the police under the Licensing Acts :—Alder- man Hutchinson, Councillor Dr, Cannel! (convener) and Councillor Heaton. It was also reeelved that two new members be appointed to make up the strength of the force, which has been reduced by twie Reservists being recalled to the colours ; that the tender of Mr. T. E. Pickton for repairs to the prison van at £l7 17s be accepted ; and that a horse ambulance be provided, and that tenders for the same be obtained. Councillor SHAW GREEN asked whether the appoint- ment of the two constables was temporary or not. The DEPUTY-MAYOR: 'I hat is So. Alderman PAIRCLOIIGH stid he did not think so,for the Chief Constable asked for two additional constables te take their places. The MAYOR said they gave their pleige to these two reserve men that their places would be kept open for them, and whether the other two new men would be kept on would be for the Council to decide. It would he a question whether it was necessary for them to be kept on but it was probable that they would be required permanently. The minutes of the committee were adopted. £22,430 TO BE BORROWED. PROPERTY OWNERS AND PRIVATE STREET WORKS. At a meeting of the Finance and Estate Committee held on the 13th November, it was resolved " that, pur- euant to a sanction of the Local Government Beard dated the 4th day of May, 1899, the Council do borrow from the Ecclesiastical Commissioners for Eneland the sum of £22,430 for the purposes mentioned in the said sanction, the said sum of £22,430 to be repaid with ietereet at the rate of £3 2s 6 1 per cent. per annum within a period of 50 years by equal annual instalments of principel aro! interest combined. In accordance with the res Aution Teemed at the last meeting, the Borough Treasurer submitte i a report as to the accounts owing for private street works, which showed that there was not less roan £2,385 eeerdue, upon which nothing was being paid. It ee as resolved that the Town Clerk take such steps as may b necei.siry to compel immediate payment, and that a report as te the position of negotia- tions with the Manchester and Liverpool Trausport Company, Limited, be preeented at the next meeting of this committee. In moving that the minutes of the committee be con- firmed Councillor Sa.ew GREEN said the Council would notice that they had negotiatei a loan with the Ecclesi- astical Commissioners tor a period of 50 years, and they would have no further trouble with the sum of £22,000. It would be noticed that they had had some trouole with a great many owners of property who had not made their payments in accordance with agreement. As It had become a burden it was found necessary to take some steps, and that viral why they had instructed the Town Clerk to take .proceedings against those who had not paid. Alderman PAIRCLOUGH seconded. Councillor BENNETT said he noticed that they had bound themielves to pay £3 2s 6d per cent for the next 50 years. It seemed to him a big figure, as they had borrowed Sums at a lower rate than £3 21 63. Alderman PRANCOMB asked whether the people who owed this £2,000 were paying as much interest as they themselves were paying. The MAYOR: They are paying us four per cent. Aldermen FRANCOMB : I don't think we should be too hard on these people. Councillor Snew GREEN said the question raised by Councillor Bennett had been under serious consideration for some time. They had borrowed that money for a period of 50 years and there would be no renewal, no stamps and no more ttouble. They would be able to pay by annual instatments,and they thonght under tho pre- sent condition of things it was an excellent bargaiudThis sum of £2,385 for street works was overdue, and it had become a serious burden not only upon the Council, but upon the committee who saw to the financing of this particular thing. It gave a great deal of trouble to keep upon the books. 'There was a time when tho money had to be paid straight off, but under the present circum- stances they had endeavoured to meet the wishes of those who had not been able to pay, but unfortunately they had taken advantage of the Council's leniency. The minutes were confirmed. DELAYS AT LA.TCHFORD SWING BRIDGE. At a meeting of the Street Improvement and Lighting Committee it was resolved that the sum of £250 be paid to Messrs. Greenall, Whitley and Company. Limited, for the purchase of a strip of laed in Old Loadon-road, near the Saracen's Head, containing 88 square yards,and now occupied by three houses which are to be taken down, and that the Corporation purchase one half in width Of the north gable of Messrs. Totes new property in Bridge- street. In moving the confirmation of these minutes Alderman SUTTON said he thought it would be a very desirable improvement near the Saracen's Head, and, therefore. Use committee had agreed to purchase. With regard to the purchase of the north gable of Messrs. Toft's new property in Bridge-street he would point out that owing to the re-building of the Feathers Hotel it would become a party wall and the object of that resolution wae,there- fore, that the Corporation should have power to pur- chase a half share in the wall if they thought 'fit. The matter had been referred to Mr. William Owen, aad if heneported that, in his judgment, it would tee advan- tageous for the Corporation to purchase they notelet do so. Alderman BOLTON seconded. Councillor PIERPOINT said he wished to call the atten- tion of the Council to the serious interruption of traffic that took place through the swinging of the Latchford Swing Bridge. Of course, if it were only for five minutes that the rights of the travelling public were taken away he wotild not have occasion to grumble,but when they found that their rights were taken away to the extent of 20 minutes, then he thought it was quite time to interfere. (Hear, hear.) He thought he had a perfect; right to ask that Council, in its goodness to prevent more or lees what he thought was a public scandal. (Hear, hear.) For instance, that morning they were stopped 20 minutes.and the excuse given was that there was a fog. They could not help it if there was a fog. There was no reason why they sheuld be kept. Let them tie their ships up. (Laughter.) Another time a ship got between the two piers of the bridge and refused to go one way or the other. He thought it was time that that important borough should look after its rights, and, in coajunctiou with the County Council, bring about a proper state of things. (Hear, hear.) It was simply abominable. The MAYOR: This matter will be brought before the notice of the proper committee, and such steps taken as we possibly can. ColltlefflOT PIERPOINT lam much obliged. The minutes were then carried. HEALTH COMMITTEE. A NEW REMEDY FOR INSANITARY PROPERTY. The following reeolutions were adopted at a meeting held on the 15th and 29th November :—That the follow- ing members be appointed a sub-committee for the purposes of the Housing of the Working Classes Act . The Chairman, Deputy-Chairman, Councillors Baird, Greening, Plumpton and Wilkinson. It was resolved that John Church, James Powell, arid Walter Thomas Flood, be appointed inspectors of neisances of the borough. It was also decided that, for the purpose of more effectively carrying out the work under the Hous- ing of the Working Classes Act and the Public Health Acts. the Borough Surveyor be requested to arrange for an officer of his department to prepare plans and speci- fications in accordance with instructions of the Medical Officer of Health, showing the work necessary to render habitable houses condemned by the Medical Officer of Health. In moving the confirmation of these minutes Alder- man Sutton said with reference to the carrying out of the Working Classes , Act arid the Pmhflc Health Ac':

would explain thet in many case where pee•feries had been condemned by the Meeical Offi yer elf itealee a.a in- sanitary dvrellings,the owners of property had experssad their willingness to do all that Wag necessary to put these houses in proper tenantable pliicion provilioe:they were informed what work was require!. (Bear, bear.) • The Town Hall Park, and Baths Committee have pissed the following resolutions :—That a leese of the iand required by the volunteers for exteneions and im- provemente (with the exception of the land for the ex- tension of a leB3 Room) be granted for a term of 14 years ; that the alterations to Bank House required by the Water Department be carried out, subject te that department paying an increased rent of 5 per cent upon the Cost ;that the wall of the park at the corner of Oros- field-street and Froghall.lane be sA back in accordance , with the plan approved; Messrs. Greeeall, Whitley and Co., Limited, hiving agreed to sell the Corporation a strip of laud at the opposite corner of Crasfieldeetreet and Fregliall-lane at the same price that they paid for the same, that the terms b 3 agreed to and the improve- ments made. Alderman BOLTON, in moving the adoption of the minutes, said the proposed alteration at toe corner of Croefield-street would constitute a very desirahle im- provement. Messrs. Greenall,Wnitley and Co.,Licaitod, having agreed to sell the Corporation a strip of land at the opeosite corner of Crolfield-street and Froehall-lane, a grand street improvement could be effected With refereece to the qees'ion of Turkish baths, it was the intention of the committee to carry that matter through as early as poFsible. Councillor &Lisle' seeonded. • Councillor JAMES EVANS asked if it was the intention of the committee to put a gate at the fir corner of the Park. It would be a distinct improvement. That side of the town was growing very rapidly, and the com- mittee should take into consideration the desirability of carrying out such a work. 1 Councillor SMETHURST said the gate in the centre of the wall he thought should be removed to the corner. The matter was an important one. Alderman SUTTON said that when this question came before the Council before and was discussed, the objec- tion to having too many gates was stated to be that it would require more 'man to look after the Park. This matter should be properly discus:esti in committee, and any recommendations from them could then be con- sidered. His own opinion was that the fewer the gates the better opportunity there would be for keeping the Park in order. Councillor F. R. ROBERTS said he should move an amendment tothe effect that the minutes be passed with the exception of the reselution reterrine to the purchase of laud and the removal of the wall. He believed that Messrs. Greenall. Whitley and Company bought the land to build a public-house, and paid a very fancy price for

it. The MAYOR: Will you take my asauranne that our price is an extremely lo e one? Councillor ROBERTS: I don't think we ought to take anyone's assurance. (Laughter.) The MAYOR : It is not desirable to disclose the priee. It is a very low price, and it is only fair to say that it is the same price paid by Messrs. Greenall 20 years ago. I am sure I ceunot be regarded as prejedieefi in favour of Messrs. Greenall. (Llaughter.) It would be a great mis- take to allow this resolution to be rent beck. Councillor F. R. ROBERTS sail Fp) 00j,:0ted ti ti Principle of passing resolutions he did no un lereteed. It might be a very low price or not. -fe was willing, however, to lot that stand and to move that the cninutes be passed wiel the exception of the one referrieg to the wall being wit back. It seemed to him that the whole of the wall ought to come down. (Hear, bear.) They might block up the gate in Kendrick-street. It was not much use.- People living in the crowded parts of Froehall-lane had either to go along Kendrick-street or to the other end of Crosfield-street. It would be a great ' ornament in that part of the town, if they had a pair of handsorete gates at the corner. He moved an amend- ment that the minutes be confirmed with the exception of the resolution he had referred to. Councillor BENNETT seconded. He said the wall was unsightly, and they ought to remove it te make a thoroughly good job of that side of the Park. Councillor TINNION supported the amendment. He ob- jected to Alderman Sutton's remark that they ought not ta have so many entrances. His opinion was that the Park was far the public goad, and it was desirable to have as many entrances as possible so that everybody could enjoy what he considered to be a very beautiful park in the midst of a manufacturing town. Councillor SHAW GREEN sail he was anxious that they should make the Park convenient to all who used it. There were, however, two or three reasons against do- ing mere than was proposed. They would have to do it out of revenue if it cost more than £BO. The allowance they had in one of the orders was £BO. They could not put up handsome gates for that sum. They should have done first what the committee proposed• Councillor PLIMPTON supported the amendment. The cheese-paring policy which Councillor Shaw Green sug• gested would spoil the work altogether. It would cost very little more to do the work properly at once. People would find a great advantage in Wing able to enter the Park atiphet point. Alderman SUTTON observed that he entirely disagreed with the remarks made by Councillors Tinnion and Plumpton in reference tothe entrance in Keadrick-street. That entrance was used more, with the exception of the front entrance, than any other entrance in the Park. He thought it would be a great mistake to do away with that entrance, and he should certainly very strongly object to it, whether another entrance was made at the corner of Crosfield street or not. Alderman FRANCO3III observed that he had been anxious for many years to see this ugly and dangerous corner removed,and he was plea7ed that the amendment was going further than the proposal of the eetnmittse. They wanted a pair of gates at that corner. Re hoped this matter could be arranged without a division- The committee were as anxious as anyone to do all they could for the convenience of the public and the improve- ment of the Park. Alderman BOLTON pointed out that they had only a limited enfount of money. The committee were willing to do all they could in the Park and if they were pro- vided with the money would make the improvement. It would be admitted the improvement was considerable. (Hear, hear.) It would hardly be possible, as Councillor Smethurst; suggested, t) put a straight gate at a round cotter. It was decided to vote en the vestion. Eleven voted for the amendment and 16 against. The minutes were then agreed to. rtiE SHEDS IN ARPLEY-SFREE MESSRS. MAGINN'",

At a meeting of the Markets Committee held on the 13th Nlvenaber it was reported that the total income from all sources for the past four weeks was £4OB 7s 10d corre%‘ponding wriod last year £365 9i 41 ; increase; £42 1861. It was resolved that the license granted to Magian Bros., for the sale of horses at their. mart Arpley street, be renewed for six months. Councillor ROGERS moved the adoption of the minutes.

Councillor A; JOLLEY seconded. Councillor TINNION, referring to the proposed renewal of the license of M,sers Maginn Bros. asked for an ex- planation. Why was the license not granted as other licenses were, for '-a lengthened period P It wag very undesirable that the place should be licensed at all. He understood that the o alter of the land intended to let it for building purposes on the expiration of the present lease. He would move an amendment that th 9 minutes be confirmed with the exception of the one Itiating to Messrs Maginn's premises. Councillor BURTON seconded. He said that Arpley- street was not a proper place for such a business. A cattle market and abattoir should be provided, and the proper place for it was in Arpley fields. The MAYOR said the discussion was entirely eat of order. The Council had agreed by resolution to grant the request of Messrs Nialinn for five rare on condition that the place was then taken down, subject to the granting of the license by the Markets Committee from time to time. The XI trketsCemmittee were b-aind to come before them with the request for hs liaense to be renewed. Councillor BURTON: Are we bound to renew it every six months P ' The MAYOR: The Markets Committee are bound to come before us and request that it be renewed. Councillor BURTON said that some few months ago the Markets Committee sent a deputation to the health Committee with a view to joint action being taken with a view to securing land for a public abattoir and cattle market. He should like to know what had come of that. He thought it was a disgrace to the Council that the dis- trict near Arpley-street eheuld l'e irleteti with the present sheds for five years.

In answer to Councillor Monks. Tile MAYOR said that one of the objects of the com- mittee in only granting the license for six months was to provide for the contingency of the estaplistiment of a public cattle market. Councillor MONKS : Bat we hews the power of revolt- ing the original resolution. The MAYOR: By special notice. Councillor M9NKS ; That is what I wish members to understand. Alderman SUTTON considere.l they hid no power to prevent the place being used if the erection was in com- pliance with the bylaws. The TOWN CLERK Toe Corporatic,n have absel ute control over the selling of horses or cattle, and we can refuse to license these placfp. It would not, however, be right to do Se ttatil we are provided win a pablic cattle market. The minutes were then confirmed. THE OBSTRUCTIONS IN THE RIVER. At a meeting of the Riv-rs Committee held on the 20th November it was resolved that the Borough Sur- veyor be instructed to serve notices on the Manceesrer Snip Canal Camp any respecting the obstructions in the river reported by him. The minutes were confirmed, on the motion of the MAYOR, seconded by Councillor PIERPOIST. RETAINING FEE FOR FIREMEN. A meeting of the Fire Engine Committee was held on the 13th November. when it was resolved that the re- taining fee allowed to the memb rs be increased from £3 12s to £4 per annum,and that they be allowed L 6cl each instead of 13 for each practice attended ; that toe following members of the brigade be allowed to turn out at country fires, vlz :—Onesuperinteadent,one engineer, 030 sergeant, one stoker, and five men. The minutes were agreed to, on the motion of Coun- cillor SMETHWRST, seconded by Councillor PLUMPTON. In answer to C ouncillor Bennett the CHAIRMAN of the Committee pointed out that the resolution respecting country fires was in order that a number of firemen would be kept in the town in case of emergency within the Borough whilst the other firemea were away. A NEW RESERVOIR FOR WINWICK. At a meeting of the Water Committee it was reselved that a special sub-committee. consisting of the Chair- man, Deputy-Chairman, the Mayor, C.Councillors Evans, Seavr Green and M oik, be appointed to carry out tee details of the work authorized by the committee in con- nection with the waterworks extensions ; that the ten- der of Mr George Bell for the construction of a new reservoir at Winwick for. the sum of £22,048 1961 be ateeepted ; that the tender of the Glenfield Company, Limited, for the supply of valves and fittings in coonee.- ties with the reservoir at £509 18s be accepted ; that the Water Eneineer be iostracted to lay the new Bin. :mita from Wiewick to Hill Warren, and to employ the necessary laboar ; that the Water Engineer be authorized to advertise for a yeti lent eneineer at £2OO per annum ; arid that the agreement between the Cor- poration and Mr. James Parr, now oredece,l an i read by the Town Clerk, be approved, and the Town Clark authorized to sign a duplicate thereof. Alderman FRANCOMB 03-)VOd tl9 adoption of the minutes.

Councillor Los seconded. In answer to Councillor Bennett, At lerman FRANCOMB said the appointment of the resi- deet eneineer was not permanent. The minutes were coneo•mee, TIIE TRAIN SERVICE BEr 'NUN LONDON AND TEIE NOR TH. A DEPU raTroN APPOINTED. Toe foliewine resolutions have been adopted at a meeting of the General Purposes Committee : That the Mayor, Aldermen Sutton and Wright, and Councillor Monks be appointed to negotiate foe the purchese or exchange of land in Howlee, adj oining the electricity works ; that the resolution of the Town Hall, Park, and Baths Committee to grant a lease for 14 years of the land required for trio extension of the volunteer quarters be confirmed ; that a representation be made to the Linden and North-Western Railway Company with the object of obtaining a better service of trains betereen London, Warrington and the North; that the Postmaster-General he aporoached on the subject of obtaining direct tote- grannie communication with London. Toe Mavort proposed the adoption of the minutes. Alderman FRANCOMB seconded. Councillor SHAM GREEN Said it was time representa- tion was made to the railway company with regard to the poor service of traies to London. Warrington was Practically no better treated thaa Hartford in the matter of trains to and from London. He tlaougnt Warriugton deserved better consideration from the London and North-Mir:ern Railway Company. Councillor MONKS suggested that a deputation meet the local offi eats. Councillor BURTON : And I suggest that the same thine be done wrh regard to the Postmaster-General. The MAYOR: To see the local postmaster. It was suggested that one or two outside the Council might join t he deputation. The MAYOR said that the Chamber of Commerce had taken the matter up and they might join. Councillor JAIRES EVANS propose I the following depute- ' tion :—The Mayor, Councillors Monks, Crosfield, and Sna.W Green. Comic llor SMETHITIV.T srconded.
