div.p: OHRISTIVIAS READING. New Books, Magazines, Etc.

Mr. F. Marion Crawford has written a new novel, and one differing widely from any other works of his which we recollect having read, inasmuch as it deals neither with Italian characters nor people on the stage of:modern society. " Via Crucisi" (Mac- millan, 65.) is a romance of the second crusade,and like everything else from Mr. Crawford's pen it absorbs our interest from first to last. As a romance it is undoubtedly good, but we hesitate to class it among the best examples of Mr. Crawford's work. The famous author of " Saracinesca," "Katherine Lauderdale," etcaseems scarcely at home amid the historic scenes of the years 1145-50, and on the battlefields of Palestine, yet he manages to convey a very good picture of the period. The hero of the tale, Gilbert IV arde—afterwards Sir Gilbert, the Guide of Aquitaine—is a type of character which one cannot fail to admire. Possessed of high courage, honourable to a fault, steadfast and true, ha lives in the imagination as a noble descen- dant of the Norman-Saxon line, and a worthy up- holder of British valour. His anventures date from the time of his honoured father's death at the hands of a treacherous friend, and the subsequent discovery that his mother, whom he nvered, was false to her marriage vows and unworthy of his love. Then, after making a laudable endeavour to slay in fair tight the murderer of his father and be- trayer of his mother, Gilbert Wavle enters the ser- vice of Geoffrey Plantaeenet, and Eleanor,'Queen of France. The second crusade is anlultimate eveat,and initGilbert Warde wins knighthood and great re- nown. There is some desperate fighting between the great Christiaa host and the "Seljuks" in which the hero takes a prominent share, and the descriptions of the bloody combats are in Mr. Crawford's most vivid and telling style. There is a strain of love-mak- ing through the book,complicated to some extent by the psssion of Eleanor," the most beautiful woman in the world," for the handsome Englishman. He, himself, is attachedto Wearix,a friend of his youth, and daughter of his arch-enemy, Arnold de Curbeil. The story winds up in a satisfactory meaner, though we See no necessity for Mr. Crawford's sudden springing of Dunstan, Gilbert's henchman, upon the reaaer as a relative of Beatrix. Tnere are twelve illustrations to the work, drawn by Louis Loeb. On the whole they are goad, though one or two fail to depict individuals as they are conjured up by the aid of imagination and the author's text Young April" by Egerton Castle (Macmillan,. 65.,) is a story possessing a suggestive title, and one in complete accord with its breey, youthful char- acter. One thinks of " The Prisoner of Zenda " when reading " Young April" tor the events of the romance are in that mystic time and place rendered so familar to us by Mr Anthony Hope. Kings, Queens, Dukes, and Counts, whom one has never heard of, live move and have their being in a country likewise unkaown, but which apparently hovers round the borders of Prussia and Austria. 'Young April" is a sketch of one rnoatli out of the life of an

English Duke—the month preceding his majority and accession to responsibility. Escaping with bald audacity from the irksome chains of ois tutor, the Duke of Rochester goes in search of fields and pas- tures new. Truk to tell, he finds them, and for the month of April is whirled round in a chaos of adven- ture and emotion. He lives a lifetime, and experi- ences its bitternesses and joys in that brief thirty days, but withal he maintains the honour of the aristocracy to which he belongs. The incidents ef the story follow one another in rapid succession but there is no danger of the reader being cloyed with adventure Mr Castle writes vigorously, lightly, and wittily as the occasion demands, and everything in his book goes with a delightful swing. His characters are all admirable, from the philosopher, physician, and lover Spencer to the womanly, fascinating Eva, or from the boisterous, jovial Count Neuberg to the stately, beautiful, but faithless Julia de Lucena. A number of ex- ceedingly artistic illustrations by an unknown penciller add much to the book's attractiveness.— We have not previously heard of Mr. U L Silber- tad, but as he can pen a clever and original novel we should like to become better acquainted with him and his work. "The Enchanter" (Macmillan 63) is a work which should win favourin mot quarters for it combines skilful character drawing with originality of thought. Its scene is for the most part laid in some imaginary district on the English coast known as Grimshoe, and adjacent to such places as Dangy Wick, and Tofter's All Saints. History began early here, and memories of priests and necromancers of old are cherished by the simple, superstitious folk. Young Nicholas Pycroft, the future hero of the story, is a descendant of the Screeds, a family with reputed leanings to the occult and the uncanny, and as he grows up he be- comes a student of things which do not come under the comprehension of the average individual. i'ime develops his intellect until he becomes one of the savants of the country, but at the same time re- tains a charming simplicity and honesty of charac- ter. Ira Chauncey is thh name of the girl destined to play the greatest part in his life, and from being a close friend of Nick's in childhood she comes to hate him intensely and with set purpose. Again,her hate turns to the love which has long underlain it. but much happens before the consummation of marriage bells. Maledict Screed, "The Enchanter," comes into their live ad alters the current. of both so that adventures befal them in the wilds of Northern India. "The Enchanter "is an individual with a clever, but distorted intellect. He gnes through much in order to obtain manuscripts re- lating to necromancy, and practices a little of the latter himself. The name fits him welloand towards the close of his career the reader comes to regard him with a very proper horror. Nicholas Pycroft deceats his evil purposes and attains his heart's desire. These are the main outlines of the story, but there are many side lights to it which merit study. Mr. Silberrad depicts the eccentricities of country folk with a nsas..-,er hand, and some or the minor characters are really admirable. Messrs. Macmillan have issued at 6s a new and revised edition of "Impressions of South Africa," by James Bryce, which is a timely and acceptable addition to the literature on the country now in the throes of a fierce war. The new edition has been carefully revised throughout and, as far as possible, brought up-to-date by noting in their proper places, the chief events of importance that have occurred since the book first appeared in 1897. Mr Bryce has not altered, however, the historical chapters, and those which deal with recent politics, but has left the statement of his own views exactly as they were first written, be-

cause they were formed and expressed before the 1 events of the last few months, an without any references to the controversies of the moment. In a prefatory chapter he says there are conclusive reasons against attempting to continue down to the outbreak of war the historical sketch in chapters 2 to 12. The materials for the historian are still scanty and imperfect, leaving him with data scarcely sufficient for judging the intention and motives with which some things were done. Atten- tion is called to some of the salient facts that have occurred since 1896,end to some aspects of the case that have been little considered in England, and altogether Mr. Bryce's labours should be fruitful in enlightening us on the history and undercurrents of South African affairs. The work contains the Trans- vaal conventions of 1881, and 1884,and three maps. Two more excellent six shilling novels which we have received from Messrs Macmillan and Company are " Valda Ildnem," the romance of a Turkish harem by Jaisy flugh Pryce, and "Donna Teresa," by Frances Mary Peard, author of " An Interloper," "The Career of Claudia," etc. Both books are of the " Light literature " type and can be relied upon to while away a few pleasant heurs.—We have also received a copy of Tennyson's "The Peincess ' in the Golden Treasury Series, a neat little book published at 2s. 6,l.—Volume 10. the last of the" Works of Shakespeare" in the splendidly-edited and well- got-up Eversley Series is now out of the press. There is:thus clmpleted one of the finest issues of Shakes- peare ever placed before the public. "Every Man's Own Lawyer.'—We have received from the publishers (Messrs. Crosby Lockwood and Son, Lowden) a copy of the new edition for 1900— the 37th—of this popular and almost indispeniable work of reference, one of the best-known publica- tions in the kingdom. Forming a " complete epitome of the Laws of England," and published at the very appropriate price of 6i. Si.(a sum, which it is claimed on the cover, may be" saved at every consultation !"), the object of the volume is to enable those who consult it to "help themselves to the law," and thereby to dispense as far as possible with professional assistance ; and there can be no doubt that the book, if properly used will be the means of saving many a 6s. 81. to its purchasers. The "Concise Dictionary of Legal Terms," which is appended to the text, consider- ably increases the value of the work, helping to make it thoroughly intelligible to non-professional readers. The amount of information sgsseeent lite the volume is woaderfril. That it has ken awn-

piled with considerable care, is evident to all who consult its pages; and since ignorance of the law is the cause of most of its infractions, the volume should undoubtedly tend to do away with the necessity of litigation. If it were not done so well it mot contribute more to lay mistakes, but it is so plainly written that he who runs may read, and he who reads may understand. The ordinary man of business will find the leading points of law well summarised in its 750 pages; where advice is offered, it is given in a clear and judicial manner ; the matter is well arranged ; and the work is care- fully brought up to date. This latter f,?ature is a great point in a book of the kind. It is a standing feature of" Every Man's Own Lawyer," that, year by year,new judicial decisions upon interesting and important points of law are incorporated in the text, thus in all respects bringing the volume up to date. For the general reader, indeed, there is no law book so comprehensive, so intelligible, so com- plete, or so accurate.—ln Macmillan's Sixpenny Series the last numbers issued are "Carrots,"by Mrs. Molesworth, and " The Miner's Right," by Rolf Boldrewood, an interesting story faithfully de- picting life in the Australian mining camps throughout the fifties.

" The Ship of the Stars" by A.. T. Quiller-Couch (C ssell and Co., Gs.) is one of the most refreshing works of fiction we have bad the pleasure of perus- ing for some time, and when we add that it is sure to enhance the author's reputation an idea may be gathered of its quality as a novel. The scene is pitched in " Q's " favourite west country, where, in imagination, we dwell with keen pleasure and become well acquainted with the eccentric Cornish folk. No one can batter coavey to the ordinary mind the peculiarities, ruggedness, and simple charm of these people than can Mr. Quiller-Couch. Hie characters are always lifelike, and in the choleric Squire Moyle we have an individual of a not uncommon type, but at the same time one whose character lends itself to considerable embel- lishment and exaggeration without being in the least spoiled. Theophilus Raymond and Honnria both perform admirably the parts allotted to them in Mr. Couch's ,trama—a drama too that is strong in comedy. In fact the course of "The Ship of Stars" alternates pleasantly between islands of humour, currents of pathos, and rocks of tragedy. The author's versatility of conception is very strik- ing, and one, fads it just as strongly exemplified in scene pourtrayal as its character drawing. His latest book is of the class of those that are not easily forgotten and leave pleasant memories be-
bind. A r@adabl3 book i " Advanced Australia "

(fethuen and Co., 3s 6i), by Wiliiam Johnson Gall.eway,M,P. which gives a shert,general account of Australia on the eve of federation. Mr Gallo- way's journeyings in Australia and New Zealand took place in the early portion of this year so that his impressions and notes on these countries possess the merit of freshness. In his preface the author says he has attempted no more than to convey to the reader how Australia impressed a chance traveller ; as an exporter, especially, of raw produce as a possible home and outlet .for our surplus population, as a fiedd for the observatien of political experiments, and as a member, generally, of the Imperial body-politic. This much, at least,we think Mr Galloway has accomplished. Ile has evidently gone about with eyes that see, and ears that hear, and his chatty, readable, well-informed comments should be of value and interest to all who are in the least concerned about the welfare of the great Antipodean Continent. "Singing Time" (Archibald Constable and Co. ss) is far and away the best child's song book we have yet seen. Simple little ditties with music by Arthur Somervell, are just the things to delight childish ears. Then too, there are drawings of a very high class by L Leslie Brooke, which picture lambs frolicking, children romping, and all sorts of scenes and events which are likely to interest small minds. We must say a word for the printer who has turned the book out in superb style, so that in addition to being a children's treasure it is in no small degeee a work of art. Parents cannot do better than in- vest in "Singing-Time" if they wish to find a novel and suitable present for the youngsters.—We have also received too late for detailed notice in this issue "Janice Mereigh," (Constable 6s) a story of the American Revolution, by Paul Leicester Ford ; and " Sunningevell" (Constable 6e), by F. Warre Cornish,. "Tire StrandjMagazine" for December is a bulky double number containing 208 pages and 250 illustra- tioas all for one shilling. Mr. Coaau Doyles short but eventful story in three parts "The Greeley Master," is comp eted,and the same announcement is made with re- gret iTn regard to "Stories of the Sanctuary Club," by L. f. Meade and Robert Eustece. We could have perused another half-dozen of these semi-scientific, wholly ab- sorbing and tragic tales without having too much of a good thing. The number contains also an illustrated interview with Sir Lawrence Alma-Tadema, R A., articles on "Signalling in the Navy," "Are Indian Jugglers Humbugs," "Christmas Day inthe Army," etc. etc. Among the contributors eif stories, sketches and the like, are Robert Barr, Stephen Crane, Grant Aden, G, Manville Fenn. E Nesbit, and A Conan Doyle.— " Unbeaten Tracks in Japan," is another new publication by Messrs Newnes,whicta call' be completed in eight parts The author is Mrs. Bishop, and her interesting record of tramps in the interior will cantain a map and 56 illustra- tions. The numbers are ioase,i at 6d.—Bovs must not miss the Christmas number of "The Captain," which front cover to cover is full of thrilling yarns and splen- did articles. Oae of the latter is a Boer's account of Majuba which will be read with deepened interest owing to the present war. Contributors to the columns of the Captain include Kahle Howard, (who interviews Mr. Manville Fenn), John Mackie, C Hubert Wolff, C B Fry, Fisher Vane, Fred I/Meuse, Louis Wain, R S Warren Bell, and others.—" The Wide World Magazine " is another double number possessing good value for the money. It abounds in startling narratives, thrilling escapes, bloodcurdling experiences, and accounts ol strange sights. Better (natter for perusing over the Yule leg could not be imagined. " Battles of the Nineteenth Century" is being re-issued by Messrs.Casssll and Co.,in 7d numbers. With Part 1, is given away an excellent map of South Africa, printed in colours, while a carefully prepared illustrated history of the war in the Transvaal commences in Part 2,—There are increasing siens of enterprise in the pro- duction of " Cassell s Magazine," one of the best monthlies ever published. The Christmas number of , this magazine is a treasury of attractive art and in- teres.ting literature. " Ths For:une Teller," a Rsmbrandt photogravure from the painting by R 0 Coeke,exhibited at the Royal A. cademy this year, forms a very artistic plate, given as a aupplerneet ; but in addition to this special feature the magaziao contains three other pic- tures of similar production, besides full-page drawings of excellence. It is denbtful if art has ever been dis• played more strikingly in a magazine than in this in- stance. Then in the 160 pages of the Christmas number there is to be found an abandance of interesting and entertaining contributions, from the Marquis of Lorne, who writes crisply about "Windsor Castle", &T Quiller- Couch (" Q.") M C Selman (describing Sir Henry Irving : Tee Man and the Artist"), W L Alden, Tighe Hopkins,Max Pembsrton,S R Crockett,Ouide,aud other writers of note.—" Uncle Tom's Cabin" is being issued by Messrs Cassell and Go. in eight sixnennv Darts. It is well printed and well iliustrated. —"The Quiver" for Decem- ber is accompanied tw i-s popular literary supplement " Christmas Arrows," the stories in which easily up- hold the reputa%ieu of the magazine. Both are excellent Eixpennyworths —"The Iron Pirate." by Max Pember- ton is tlie. latest of Messrs. Cassell's sixpenny paper- backed novels. The Current Number of" Bibby's Quarterly."—'( Liver- pool), con:ains a facsimile reproduction ot the M.S. of Kiplinea famous poem, " The Absent-Minded Beggar." It will be remembered Chit Mr. Joseph Bibby purchased the M S. for £250.
Warrington Field Club.

At the fifth meeting of the session, Dr. Bowden delivered a lecture on water. After a brief historical sketch of the various moles of supplying large populations with water for both drinking cleansing and trade purposes, from Roman to modern times, the lecturer proceeded to describe the various sources whence water is or has been obtained and the methods of distribution. In passing he in- dicated the possibilii.ies of pollution either at the source of supply or by reason of defects in the apparatus of distribution; the dissemination of gertu diseases,the more o. less effectual effmts at purifica- tion, the folly of faith in filters, and the need and means for chemical and microscopical examination of drinking waters were successfully described with lucidity and without any parade of learning,though the learning was there. In the discussion which followed the doctor WAS warmly congratulated on the scientific skill with which he had marshalled and presented the facts. The President, Councillor J. Shaw Green, in closing the debate, expressed t'ae wish tbat both his colleagues on the Water Com- mittee and the public generally might have had the privilege of hearing and enjoying Dr. Bowden's admirable and suggestive address.

div.head: FATAL FLAW.
div.p: A FATAL FLAW.
County Council Election at Daresbury. Mr. John Ockleston Elected.

The last day on which nominations could be handed in of candidat .8 for the vacancy in the repreFentation of the Daresbury Division on the Cheshire County Council, occasionei by the resignation of Mr. E trp was Satur- day last. Mr. Hibbert, as representing Mr. R. Potts, clerk of the County Conned, at:ended at the Diresbury Schools for rho purpose ot receiving nominations and hearing objections to the same. Mr. John Ockleston, J. P.,tanner, of Oakdal,:.Overton, was proposed by Henry Reynolds, seconded by Joseph H. Salkeld; also proposed b W Wallington, seconded by C W Phillips ; also proposed by Samuel Taylor (Run- corn), seconded by Thomas Ford; also proposed by Edward Aaron, seconded by H Branch. Mr. Hatton Wright, Crofton Lodge, Kingsley, fanner, was proposed by Peter Tickle. seconlel, by James C priestly; other nomination papers wore also handed in on his behalf. Mr. T H Annett, acting as agent for Mr Ockleston lodged an objection to the first nomination paper on behalf of Mr. Wright on the ground that no such name as James C Priestly appeared on the electors roll.

A reference to the list revealed the fact that Mr. Priestly was described simply as James Priestly and not James C Priestly. The objection was upheld, and the nomination of Mr. Wright was thus invalidated. The result is that Mr. Ockleston succeeds to the position vacated by Mr. Earn without the turnilil of an election.

HOSPITAL SUNDAY.
MEETING OF THE COMMITTEE.

A meeting of the Hompital Sunday Committee was held in the Infirmary on Friday. Mr. John Fairclough presided and there were also present: Revs. Jaines Davies, E R Tarbuck, J S Hughes, ti Drummond, Fathers Whittle and Wilson and Mr A J Jolley (hon sec) THE SECRETARY'S REPORT.

Mr A J JOLLEY in his report said that four places of worship which contributed to the Hospital Sun- day Fund in 1898 failed to do so in 1899. One church recommenced contributing and on the balance there was a net gain of 17s 6i under these heads. The total receipts have been £247 us 84 a decrease as compared with last year of £l7 3s Bd. The ex- penses had been for advertising £lO 108 ;for station- ery and postages £3 9s Od a total of £l3 19s as compared with £l4 lOs in 1898. The Rev FATHER WHITTLE proposed the. adoption , of the report. The Rev JAMES DAVIES seconded. The Rev. W. a DRUMMOND thought the com- mittee ought not to let the fact that a diminished amount had been collected pass without notice. It could hardly be considered satisfactory that with an increased population there was a smaller amount collected. It was a fairly big drop from £261 15s 4d to £247 us 84 this year. He believed it was due to some extent to the wealthier people going outside the town. One would naturally expect that the churches in the district would send larger contributions in consequence, but, that did not seem to be the case. The SECRETARY said that with two or three exceptions there had been a small shrinkage in the amounts collected and this was raore noticeable in the churches outside the Borough than those in- side. He was sorry there was nat as much en- thusiasm shown as might be expected on humani- tarian grounds. The CHAIRMAN said they had been round the town getting further subscriptions and tbat might have interfered with the collections. The Rev. FATHER WILSON thought the Nursing Association might have affected them a little. The report was adopted. RE-ELECTION OF SECRETARY.

The Rev. W. H. DRUMMOND proposed the re- election of Mr A J Jolley as hon. secretary. He came in contact with him in connection with other important works and he was Acquainted with Mr Jolley's aptitude for business. He did not think they could have a better secretary. The Rev. JAMMS DAVTES seconded, and proposed a vote of thanks to Mr. Jolley for his services. The Rev. Father WHITTLE supported, and the resolution was unanimously carried. Mr. A. J. JOLLEY, in accepting the position and acknowledging the vote of thanks, said it gave hini a great deal el pleasure to be able to do what he could in a humble way for the benefit of the insti- tution, and he hoped what had been said would help to increase the contributions both inside and outside the town. (Hear, hear.)

Ax Y crusade against the Humanity in British Army, deigned to War.

_ show that it violates the best usages and traditions of war, would be most un- fortunate at the present moment. We cannot believe that there is any real foundation for some of the charges which are being made. That in the heat of battle, after the enemy has been driven into retreat, it may be found that soldiers have taken the fullest advantage of th&r position to inflict severe losses upon a broken foe, is not in- humanity. It is part of the business of war to make the best use of every opportunity to cut up a demoralised enemy. When positions have been captured and the defenders are in full flight, cavalry is usually launched against them to complete the victory, and whatever injury they inflict must be reckoned as a part of the engagement. It is no more inhuman to slaughter a flying foe than it is to pound a position with artillery and capture it at the point of the bayonet. Where- ever there have been abuses of the white flag by the beaten troops, the conquerors cannot be ex- pected to display a Christian forbearance and to spare the retreating force. War is, at its best, a terrible business, and now that some of its horrid details are brought home to us by the pens of des- criptive writers, we roust preserve our calmness, and not allow ourselves to be moved by feelings of protest and disgust. Still, there are limits to even this philosophic equanimity, and we shall never cease to protest upon firing on the wounded, on the ambulance men, and upon the hospitals and non-combatants. A bom- bardment is always a sad business, because it exposes inhabitants to the same perils as com- batants. If at Mafeking, Kimberley, and Lady- smith there have been injuries done to private houses and civilians have been killed, we cannot fairly complain. These things are part of the horrors of war, and they fall heavily upon many people who are entitled to our sympathy and res- pect. The time may come when British shells may have to be fired into Boer towns, and then the civilians must suffer ii they ,:emain in beleagured places. If we make no protest now, we can listen to no protests when they may be made by the other side. In the treatment of the wounded there is no room for complaint. The Boers have done their best for the British wounded who may have fallen into their hands, and our medical men and nurses have been as kindly to the Boer wounded as they have been to their own countrymen. There is plenty of evidence on either side to make any hysterics about partiality entirely beside the mark. It has been found that some of the British wounded have been hit by bullets of many kinds, some of

which are generally used for sporting purposes, and expand on impact. As to the prisoners, there have been complaints, but we have only heard one side, because communication with the British prisoners at Pretoria has been oi a very irregular and indefinite character. The Boer prisoners are mainly on board ship at Simon's Town, and the best arrangements for their comfort and sustenance have been made that are possible under the circum- stances. Probably as much may be said of the British prisoners at Pretoria, if their dietary has been somewhat unsatisfactory. It will be a great mistake, however, if isolated irregularities are seized upon to begin aseries of imputations against British soldiers and British officers, the better to stimulate sympathy for the Boers who aro invad- ing Britisl4 territory.
THERE are some significant The Free State, indications that tho Orange

Boers have almost had enough of the war. Some of their troops left the Modder River before the battle was over, amidst the jeers of the Transvaalers, and now we learn that an unofficial mission may come to this country to sound the Government as to what terms the Orange Boers can obtain—in lopendence is what they want—if they discontinue the war, as far as they are concerned. It is within the power of President STEYN,WhO has been one of President KRUGER'S worst friends,to recall the Orange Boers from the field, and to remain neutral for the remainder of the war. If he will not do that he is not entitled to be dealt with by separate negotiations. He had been for years preparing for the war, enlisting the services of a German officer of artillery to organise drill, and arm the. Free State artillery against this country, because no other object for the work is conceivable. Had he not promised the Transvaal Executive his aid, and had they not known what steps he had been taking to make that aid valu- able, we strongly doubt whether any war would have accrued, and certainly there would have been no invasions of British territory. Under these circumstances the Orange Boers, who are still at war with us, cannot expect to be dealt with apart from their allies, or to obtain more favourable terms when the settlement comes. They were no parties to the quarrel, except as they made them- selves so. We had no grievances to adjust in which they were directly concerned, and their participation in the war was a wanton dis- turbance, which will have to be punished by the same means as will be retorted to in order to punish the attack on the British position. In interna- tional law, in fact, their position is worse than that of the Transvaal, and it would not be expedient to grant them better teims unless they made some sudden and striking change of policy at once, cal- culated to bring the war to an early and a decisive end. If the Orange Boers were to say that they would withdraw all their troops from British terri- tory unless the Boers retired into the Trans- vaal, and at once sued for peace, the situation would become one worthy of some consideration. To negotiate a separate peace with them whilst they are still fighting on British territory, and lending their aid to the Transvaalers, would be most injurious, and it would even be worth describing as suicidal. We have given to the Orange Free State its independ- ence, and it has employed it so badly that the first time we were in a tight placo it casts its military and material aid on the side of our opponents, the invaders of British territory. Accordingly, we believe that no unofficial mission will have much success in this country, and that public opinion would not sanction the making of separate terms with a State at war with us, and affording us no striking proof of its penitent and pacific endencies:

We are all so pleased with ourselves owing to the astonishing success of the Mansion House War Fund that there is some danger of it being for- gotten that there may be very few widows and orphans to relieve at all. The bulk of the money has been subscribed for this specific object. There is over £230,000 available for the widows and orphans of those killed during the campaign, but, as might have been forseen from the fact that the large majority of our soldiers are compulsory bachelors, only twenty-seven cases have come up for relief. There have been thousands of casualties killed and wounded; it is to be feared there will be thousands more, but only an infinitesimal pro- portion will leave widows and children, and it is probable that this part of the fund will be ever so much too large for the purpose indicated. The other funds for temporarily assisting the relatives of soldiers engaged in the war and for assisting the disabled themselves, have not been so generously patronised. It is to be hoped that, if the principal fund turns out to be too big, the residue will be used wisely. The public will not care to have a repetition of the Crimea foolish- ness. There is a fund locked up to this day because it was intended for the relief of widows and orphans, and there are now no widows and orphans to speak of to relieve, though heroes who fought in person at Balaclava,lnkermann, Alma, or in the trenches, are allowed to die miserably in the workhouse without an effort being made to assist them. At the meeting of the Runcorn Board of Guardians on Tuesday reference was made to this "locked-up " Patriotic Fund, and it was decided to make an effort to obtain an allowance from it in aid of a Crimean veteran now in Dutton Work- house. Their efforts at untying the red-tape knotted round this Fund are worthy of every sup- port and merit success.

The " Liv.erpool Mercury" says "Alderman Griffiths, Mayor of Southport, who is a t 3tal abstainer, was hospitable enough to provide his guests with generous liquors at the Mayoral luncheon. By this lilerality he appears to have provoked a good deal of hostile criticism in tem- peranco circles. We are glad to notice that his worship ic quite unmoved at the sormess of his critics. He showed nice consideration in not forcing his guests to content themselves with the liquid refreshments that satisfy himself. The Mayoral office is a public one. He was not enter- taining private friends in }is own house, though there are staunch teetotalers who do not, even at the domestic board, impose their particular prin- ciples upon guests. Alderman Griffiths will have the sympathy of the overwhelming majority of the people of Southport. in standing up for inde- pendent action. That is what is really at stake. Whether he serves wines or not at mayoial lun- cheons is a matter of mulch less consequence than that a mayor should be at liberty officially to treat his guests as he thinks desirable."

These remarks, and their cause, should he of interest to Warrington people, as our present Mayor is a lifelong teetotaler and therefore placed in a position of similar awkwardness to that occupied by the Mayor of Southport. There can be no denying that it is awkward for a Mayor to possess the conscientious scruples of a teeto-taler, because nineteen out of every twenty of the people he entertains officially are drinkers to a greater or lesser extent of spirituous liquors, and would deem themselves insulted at being asked to be content with lemonade and the like. We do not know what course Alderman Roberts is likely to take, but, as a teetotaler, he has already departed from the custom of previous Mayors, in refusing to provide wines for the consumption of those who repaired to the Town Hall after the proces- sion on Mayor's Sunday. His action in this instance

is one we entirely endorse, for apart from other considerations it is not the seemliest conduct to go direct from Church and imbibe intoxicating liquors at the Town Hall. If Alderman Roberts chooses to order his banquets without the accompaniment of a wine list, then we think he deserves the com- mendation of all persons who have a respect for strict observance of principle and the voice of conscience. But though he is a teeto taler and holdb views in accord with our own, we do not see that the Mayor in his official capacity is bound to consider his personal scruples before the convenience of his guests. There is a good deal of sense in the arguments adduced by the" Mercury," which wisely draws a distinct line between civic functions and private parties. The position of Mayor is one which entails public service before anything else, and it is not unreasonable that that section of the public which is fortunate enough to share the occasional hospitality of His Worship should have their foibles, fancies, and even failings considered.

FATAL SCAFFOLD ACCIDENT AT WIDNES. At Widnes, yesterday morning, William Percival, bricksetter, aged 63, who was employed on the erection of a new shed at Bowman's Works, fell from a scaffold 25ft. high and was instantly killed. It was very foggy at the time.

div.head: IN AID OF THE WAR FUND.
div.p: IN AID OF THE WAR FUND.

A most successful concert with the above object was held at the Mersey Mission on Friday eveniog.—Mr. J. Meadowcroft presided, and the talent was principally provided by the Runcorn Dock Staff. A capital pro- gramme was submitted, and a .satisfactory sum raised for the cause espoused.

div.head: COTTAGE HOSPITAL.
div.p: COTTAGE HOSPITAL.

The Committee which has been appointed to promote a scheme for the establishment of a Cottage Hospital are pleased to hear that the United AlitAli Company's staff and workmen at Wigga Works and Runcorn Works have undertaken to contribute about £5 a week for twe!vP months. In the first instance this money will be given to the Runcorn Soldiers' Relief Fund, but after the war is over it is to be handed to the Cottage Hospital account HALTON WESLEYAN TEMPERANCE SOCIETY,

A public meeting was held in the schomroom on Thurs- day last week, Mr L Rosenberg, jour;, of Weston Point., presiding. Rev 11 Morrison spoke of the" Costliness of the Drinking Habit." and produced some startling figures. Rev El Hooper, of Frodsham Union Church, advocated Sunday closing, and referred to Bible heroes who were abstainers. The vocalists were Misses C Looker and M H Rowe, and Messrs C P Bradbury and P Rowlinson, jour., and Master J Rutter, of Runcorn. Mr T Goulden accompanied.

div.head: MERSEY MI-SION WEEKLY CONCERT.
div.p: MERSEY MI-SION WEEKLY CONCERT.

The wetkly concert was given on Tuesday by Mr. Griffith's concert party. There was a fair attendance and an excellent programme was gone through. Mr. Griffiths took the chair, and after a few remarks as to the object of the concert, called upon the following artistes :—Miss Garvie. Mr W Booth, Miss Davies, Mr J Woods, Mr Stubbs, Mr W Shaw, Mr G Knight, and Master J Rutter. FORTHCOMING LECTURE.

A lecture will be delivered on Moniay evening under the auspices of the Runcorn Evangelical Free Church Connell in Bethesda Congregational Church by the Rev. R. Veitch, M.A. (Liverpool). His subject will be " The Present Crisis:—our Free Church Solution." Mr. Joni. Wilson will take the chair at 7-30, and a collection will be taken.

div.head: WIDNES POPULAR CONCERTS
div.p: WIDNES POPULAR CONCERTS

The firs's, of the popular concerts promoted by the United Alkali Co., was given on Saturday in ths Baths' Assembly-room. There was a full house, and the chair was occupied by Mr. Max Muspratt. Violin trios were given by Messrs G Warne, T Saxon, and Mr W H JAck son. Little Algy sang a couple of humorous songs, and Messrs Burke and Moran contributed two vocal duets. Mr W J Loftbouse was the humorist of the evening, and was highly successful in his sketches, encores being de- manded for every one.

div.p: SOCIAL EVENING AT THE BETHESDA SCHOOLS.

Tbe Rev. J. Osborne presided over the social gather- ing held at.the Bethesda schoolroom on Tuesday evening when a large attendance lktened to a capable address upon the " Congregational 20th Century Fund" by the ftev. Stanley Rogers (Liverpool.) Interesting items were provided by the Timmins' Glee Party. Misses Rutter, Martin, Ada Stanway. Kenyon (Kw:corm). and Thomas (Widnes),and Messrs John Jams Lunt, W Booth. James Beck, and the Milton Congregational Glee Party Widnes. Mica Clayden recited the "Quaker Reply" to Rudyard Kipling's new poem, with effect. Refreshments were provided, and an enjoyable time spent.
A TRAP OVERTURNED IN GREENIV/LY-ROAD.

About 2-30 on Wednesday afternoon an alarming accident occurred in Greenway-road which might have been attended with serious results. The governess-car belonging to Mr. A. R. Norman was being driven up the road, when a big dog jumping and frisking in front of the pony caused it to swerve and one of the wheels collided with a lamp-post, with the result that the trap was completely overturned and the driver pitched head- long. Assistance was rendered by Mr. T. Bowyer and others and it was ascertained that no very serious damage was done to the vehicle and the driver also luckily escaped with nothing worse than a severe shake- ing.

div.head: WIDNES BOYS BIRCHED FOR THEFT:
div.p: WIDNES BOYS BIRCHED FOR THEFT:

Before the Mayor (Alderman G I Neil) and Alderman S Sadler, at Widnes Police Court on M3nday, John McCarthy (12), and James Cleary (Is), were charged with stealing a box of chocolate, value 33 . the property of John Naylor from a van in Oxford-street, on Thurs- day—Complainant, a camfectionfr of Queen-street, War- rington, said that he was with the van in Oxford-street, Widnes on Thursday,which he left opposite Mrs. Riley's. When he came out he missed a box of choollates, and gave in format;on to the police.—Margaret Stanton,about ten years of age saw Cleary go into the van and take a box of toffee out and then run up the street. Witness added that on Sunday Cleary said he would "punch her two eyes nut."—P C. Davidson deposed to apprehending the prisoners.—ln answer to the charge McCarthy said " I was with Cleary when be stole it," and Cleary said, " I took it from the van. and McCarthy was with me, and helped me to eat it."—Cleary was ordered to receive 12 strokes with the birch, anl was cautioned about threatening the girl Ftanton, McCarthy was ordered to receive six strokes. RUNCORN HARRIERS.

The Runcorn Harriers visited Halt in View Harriers on Saturday, turning out from the Bee Hive, Simms Crois. The weather was gloriously fine, and the district very favourable for cross-country sport. Great interest was taken in the run, inasmuch as Halton View defeated Runcorn a fortnight ago, after Runcorn getting the two first men in, by 10 points. Both clubs were fakir well represented, above 40 runners turning out for a spin of about seven miles, over well-chosen country. It was decided to have a mile break for the finish. The run- ners lined up about one mile from home. A good race was witnessed for the finish between Sandlands and Lightfoot of the home team and Hopkins of the visitors. The following are positions of teams :—Halton View: 1, Saw-Bands; 3, Lightfoot; 7. Linaker ;8, Timperlev :11, 0. Nield ; 12, Inn" ; to'al, 42 points. Runcorn: 2. Hoo- kin.; ; Bat ; 5. Cadman ; 6, Thomas ; 9, Hill; 10, Goodall; total, 36 p-ints—a win for Runcorn by six points. This is the first defeat Halton View have sus. tamed sincel:hefformation of the club.

div.head: VOLUNTEER SATURDAY NIGHT CONCERT
div.p: VOLUNTEER SATURDAY NIGHT CONCERT

The first of a series of Saturday night concerts, given by the Runcorn Detachment of the 2nd Earl Che,hire Volunteers, in aid of the local fund for the relief of soldiers' wives and families, was given at the Drill Ha—. last Saturday evening. The chair was taken by Captain G. F. Ashton. and there was a large and enthusiasth audience. " lolanthe " by the Band pioved a capital overture. The Li-aker Party (Misses )naker and Messrs. C. E. Linaker and Lieutenant W. G. Linaker, Fredsham) contributed several items : "The old woman that lived in a shoe" was followed by " The Chamber of my Love " as an encore. " But it is so " and " Good night, beloved " were also given by the same quartette, and received spontaneous recalls. Miss Tern- oerley gave a " Serenade "as a violin solo, but achieved greater suCe,'Els as a mandoline player in the second part. Mr. Jack Rutter proved the star of the evening, and though down for but one song "Scarlet and Blue" had to contribute two other; before the audience would release him. The s-mgs were both patriotic ones. Mr H Branch contributed " Admiral Tom" (encore " Powder Monkey Jim "), and "The Soldiers of the Queen," in his usual style. A selection " Sang; of England " by the band proved greatly enjoyable, its moat enhancing movement being the:Welsh air "Hail away," the piece bin g• well re- received. It n.ight be well to suggest that the hand re- duce it; volume for future efforts, as in the double forte movements within the confines of the hsll little of the music could b- heard with effect. Mr. J. Parry sub- mitted " Let me like a soldier fall." Mrs. S. D• Matthewii followed with the old favourite "Punchinel'o." A feature of the evening was the recitation of " The Absent Minded Beggar " by Miss Agres Davies. at the close of which there was a special collation. The effi. cient accomranist was Mr. William Cooke.—On the motion of Captain Ashton a hearty vote of thanks was accorded to all who had contributed to the succ(rs of the evening.—A most enjoyable and successful rsntrhe was brought to a close by the band p'ayheg " God save the queen."

THE TRANSPORTER BRIDGE TO WIDNES.

The Law Clerk said that documents and plans of the proposed transporter bridge to Widnes from Runcorn had been deposited with the Cluncil. It was intimated that the Company had a working model of the bridge, which would most likely be brought to Runcorn and put on view. Up to the present, how- ever, the Bill had not been advertised.
RUNCORN NOTES.
[BY A CORRESPONDENT.]

One shilling a week has been given—so I learn— as a modicum of relief to a soldier's wife from the coffers of the Runcorn Relief Committee. What a mockery! The Government have decided that 7,1 shall be their allowance to all who claim from them and all else they—the poor women, can earn they are welcome to. Why does not the local committee look at the thing in the same light ? Perhaps, al- together, there are but 20 reservists gone from our district, and if they were all married, and is per wife is the figure of Runcorn's generosity, then the public have not discharged their responsibility by a great deal. Why,the woman's next door neighbour would pay that! I would suggest that the Admin- istration be slightly altered to a more generous figure if the subscriptions allow of it.

There have been rumours about that the woman Harrop—who was missed some time ago,and whose body was found in the canal, and duly buried—is still alive, and I myself have interviewed people who assert they have seen her, in the flesh, and spoken to her; and who hold the opinion that the body picked up from the canal must be that of another woman who mysteriously disappeared pre- viously. The rumour has, however, been officially contradicted by Mr. F. J. Norman, at the concert on Wednesday night,when he characterised bhe rumour as the creation of imagination. Subsequently. I again interviewed my informants, but they re- assert their confidence in their statecrents.

It is amusing to see iv the Urban District Coun- cil the battle between "gas and electricity" which is taking place just now. Of course, it would be very uncharitable to point to the" Gas-men " and the" Electricians," individually; but they are there and give expression to their opinions, so recently as yesterday, when Mr. Wilson delicately charged some of the members with " trimming their sails." Mr. Imison took exception to the remarks, and assured the Council that the ratepayers knew why he sat upon that Council and his interest in the Gas Works did not weigh with him one iota.—Mr. Wilson withdrew unreservedly his remarks as hav- ing reference to Mr. Imison, or to anyone who made like avowal to the remarks of Mr. Imison.—Mr. Handley and Mr. Grine then denied being actuated by any interest but the interest of the ratepayers, and for the time being the matter dropped.—Now, someone has been unkind enough to suggest that it is not all pure disinterestedness on the other side. Perhaps it was another case of " pot calling the kettle black."

The question of the Transporter Bridge across the Mersey is one that is taking up a little attention' The idea no doubt is a good one, but it has its dis- advantages. A far more feasible scheme, and one of greater utility would be a road bridge across from Widnes to Wiggs kettle black works, and thence across the already existing swing bridge over the Ship Canal. There is no need to go 75 feet high for a span these days; 25 to 30 feet is ample and as for the Manchester Ship Canal the swing bridge obviates any height at all. Of course the cost of erection would be greater than for a trellised' transporter bridge; but, the cost of maintenance, would be far less ; and this, coupled with the greater convenience, is an importint factor for con- sideration.

ENGAGEMENT OF AN ELECTRICAL ENGINEER. LIVELY DISCUSSION.

The Highways and Buildings Committee recommended that Messrs. Medhurst. Kitchin and Page, Consulting Rectrical Engineers, Manchester, be engaged at a tee of thirty guineas, to report generally on the provision of electricity for lighting and power purposes, to report on the offers of the firms which have offered to take over the Provisional Order, the offer of the Castner-Kellner Company, to supply electricity in bulk, to advise on the feasibility of the electric lighting of streets and the ad- visability of combining a refuse destructor with the electric lighting scheme ; the fee to include out of pocket expenses and to merge in the cscamission of five per cent. on the capital outlay in the event of being re- tained to carry out a scheme. Mr. J Wilson,in moving the adoption of the Highways and Buildings Committee minutes which included the above, said he did so as Mr. Samuel Taylor was absent. He was supporting the resolution of the Committee although he fat that he would like to have made some remarks not exactly in harmony with the resolution. Mr. George Hewitt seconded the adoption of the minutes.

Mr. W Handiey said he should like to suggest that Mr. Wilson and Mr. Hewitt take the above minute back for further consideration. There was no need or occasion for any great hurry in the matter. Indeed they had other communications from Bennett, and Ward Thomas, of a scheme, which he felt would affect the whole question of their electr:c lighting from a very different standpoint. He further pointed out that in the matter of the engagement of an engineer a neighbouring town in the same position were not rushing like they appeared to be. Mr. Grief) agreed with Mr Handle 7, ad was prepared t) second him if he put his remarks into a resolution.

Mr. Handlpy : I simply appeal to them. Mr Wilson again explained that be was in the position of Mr Taylor whom he was not aware would be absent, and under the circumstances he wished to be loyal to the committee. He did not feel inclined to take it back, but if that was the expression of the Councii,he would do so.

Mr. Bisbrown objected to the minute, on the ground that the Council 114 d by resolution sanctioned !In expen- diture of 25 guineas as ample for the engagement of an expert, and the minute of the Committee was for 5 guineas more. _
SuosQquently Mr. Hau(Hey proposed and Mr. Grice seccnden the omission of the minute.

Mr. Gatiey thought it was simply an attempt to shelve the matter,and could not understand why two members should require to refer the matter back without sub- mitting very definite reasons. Neither could Mr. Dean traderstand the wisdom of the course proposed.

Mr. Imison thought that one reason at any rate had been supplied by Mr. Wilson, who had practically told them that he would have moved some modification of the minute had he not been obliged ta take Mr. Taylor's place without notice. He was also in sympathy with Mr. Bisbrown regarding the question of expense. Again he wished to caution them about incurring thlie expenses without the consent of the ratepayers. Mr. J. W. Lightburn took it that what Mr Handley aimed at was for theaa t 3 have time to see what became of th-3 Bennett and Ward Thomas scheme before they decided upon the engagement of the engineer. Mr. Handley : That is so.

The Chairman pointed out that in accordance with minute 1544 of the Highway and Buildings Committee they were authorised to engage an engineer, and that that very minute was proposed by the very gentlemen who opposed the minute before them. He failed to see how the application of Bennett and Ward Thomas affected the scheme at all. He thought if anything it was rather a factor in favour of the earring out of the original idet that an engirver should be appointed. IF they went on like that, it could be nothing else but shelving.

Mr. Wilson in replying argued that it was noles- sary to have something tangible to place b !fore the rat-payers. The only way out of the diffilultv vv,),l to get a moor upon which to work. Mr. Wilson went on to explain that there was something said in the offer about a refuia destructor, and if they could get informa- tion about that for the extra £s,they would be benefit- ted and the money would be well earned. On appeal to the Chairman, Mr. Wilson was rated out of order.

The resolution that the minutes be passed was then carried, seven voting for and six against. Mr. Imison then moved the following amendment, " That the eriginal minute be substituted by the follow- ing ,—" That Mr. T. L. Miller, of Liverpcol. be engaged at a fee of £26 5s to report generally on the provision of Electricity for lighting and power purposes, to report en cffers of firms which had offered to take over the Provisional Order, the offer of the Castner-Kellner Co. to supply electricity in bulk, to advise on the feasibility of the E'ectric Lighting oF Streets. The fee to include out of pocket expenses and to merge in the commission of five per cent on the capital outlay in the event of be - ing retained to carry out a scheme. Mr. D Bisbrown seconded. On being put to the vote 7 were in favour of Mr. Imison's motion, and 6 against. The minutes were then agreed to. ELECTRIC RAILWAY. -A ROSY OFFER.

The following letter was also submitted to the Council by the Highways and Buildings Committee :-13, Vic- toria Buildings, Manchester, 24th November, 1899. E. Marshall, Esq., secretary to the U.D.C., Runcorn. Dear sir, with a view to promoting a scheme of electrical tramways, under the Light Railways Act, between Wes- ton. through Runcorn, Norton, Acton Grange, Moore, Walton (Inferior)and Warrington,we beg to ask whether such a scheme would receive the assistance of your Council, in any application we might make to the Board of Trade. The idea is to run the ordinary trolley system of electric trams, similar to those working in Liverpool, Leeds, and elsewhere, and when occasion requires to at- tach an additional car for merchandise and goods ; arrangements to be made with your Council to supply the electric current for the working of the system, within say two miles radius of your town. It is proposed to enter into further negotiation with the propes.d New Bridge Codpany, to run a branch route over to Widnes. The route chosen in your district will be entirely in accordance with your wishes. We send you an ordnance survey, showing the proposed route in red, but subkct to any alterations as to route you may require. If this scheme can be brought to maturity, the financial success of your Electric Light Station is assured. We have had a very considerable experience in Central Station work, and we know that if the electrical machinery can be utilized during the day, when the light is not required, the load factor is materially increas.d, and the cost of unit production is very much reduced. The average load factor obtaining in Electric Light Stations is only 10 per cent., but given an output for traction purpos:s during the day. this is easily increased to 20 per cent. This means that for lighting only the average works cost to produce a 8.0. T. Unit is 2d but with lighting and tree ion combined the cost ,s reduced to ld. Now aroume the ranital cost of you: electric lightineschemc to be £20,000, and that you sell at 51 per unit the average amount of electrieity which obtains forthis expenditure, this cc:fluid meaa 120,000 8.0 T. unite per annum, or £2,509 The Traction Company would require a mini- mum of 200,000 units per annum, which, sellino 2:1 per unit,would bring in an additional revenue nf £1,666. Total revenue for lighting and traction £4166, cost for ...mgt. nil, waste, water, repairs and maintenance. 320,000 units at 141, £1875; interest and sinking fond oo £20,039. £llll. total £llBO ; rent, rates, taxes,office, legal &c, say £lBO, profit £lOOO. For liohting only, your station would only post pay its way, if that, but with the traction combined we would ouarantee a minimum profit of £l,OOO a year- If your Council should consider this matter, we should be glad. We would, however, like to be consulted when the time is rip for ordering your engine and dynamo plant. in order that the came may be applicable to both traction and lighting. Our Mr. Bennett will be glad to wait, upon your Council to go into this matter at your convenience. —Yours faithfully, BENNETT & WARD THOMAS

div.head: TERMS OF THE LO&N
div.p: THE TERMS OF THE LO&N

The Public Works Loan Board wrote et.ating that they would advance the loan of £916 at 3 per cent interest, to be repaid in 20 years. This was considered satisfactory. HOARDS OF GUARDIANS AND THE TRANSVAAL WAR. . . .

The Clerk to the Poplar Union forWarae—dThe'loTiow- ing resolution for the Runcorn Union's consideration and support "That seeing the South African War has already left a large number of women and children de- pendent on public charity and at the close a much Larger number will be so dependent, and as private charity has never yet after any of our wars adequately provided for those whom such wars have left either as dependents or cripples, this Board is of opinion that all Boards of Guardians throughout the country should jo'n in petitioning the Ctianc.llor of the Exchequer to at once take the necessary steps for providing a sufficient sum of money from National sources for—(1) adequate main- tenance for soldiers' and sailors' wives and children (now being partly maintained by private charity); (2) ad,quats maintenance for all disabled soldiers and sailors ; (3) adequate maintenance for the widows and orphans of all soldiers and sailors."

The Chairman thought the course suggested in the resolution was the right one to adopt. Their soldiers went abroad for their country's good and to fight their battles, and it was a pitiful thing to find that when these men came home from war they were badly pro- vided for.and they became chargeable in many instances to the different unions. Personally he was strongly in favour of making their provision a matter of a national charge. (Hear, hear.) Mr. Norman thoroughly sympathised with the chair- man's remarks. They had in the Workhouse a Crimean veteran who, as far as he could gather, had borne a very mod character. He was not a man who had spent tps money in drink, and he had always been willing to work. His (Mr. Norman's) feeling was that it wag a scandal that such a man should be allowed to go to the WorkhouEe, and he thought some of the money that was being raised ought to be ear-marked for the benefit of those who were in such circumstancei. The Chairman said the Patriptic Fond had £BOO,OOO which was un-used, and yet they had people in the Workhouse. (Shame.) In reply to questions the master said the veteran in the house was over 70 years of age. ;He was a decent old man.

Mr. Linaker sad he was a hard-workitm well con- ducted man. Could not an application be made to the governors of the Patriotic Fund on his behalf? He pro- posed that the Clerk make inquiries as to whether the veteran could not be helped from the fund. Mr. Stokes seconded. He thought it was very hard that these men should be left to perish in the Work- house.
Mr. Taylor thought there must be some mistake about the disposal of that fund.
Mr- Norman pointed out that if the Clerk mad: inquiries it would lead to an explanation as to tha exact position of the fund.

The resolution was passed, and it was decided, on the motion of Mr. Norman, seconded by Mr. Edwards, to support the resolution of the Poplar Unioß. APPEAL AGAINST ASSESSMENT.—A YEW DEPARTURE. The Guardians of the PrEscot Union forwarded a copy of the following resolution which they asked the Runcorn Guardians to support :—"That the jurisdiction of Quarter Sessions in appeals against assessments should be abolished, and that all rating appeals be made to a special tribunal, to be created for that burporne. RS is recommended in the report of the Royal Commission on Taxation in the case of special properties. Mr. Mclntyre said the Assessment Committee had considered the matter, and recommended that the 'Council should support the proposal so far as it affected the valuation of railways, canals, and other public works. They were in favour of all appeals in these cases being referred to a special court instead of Quarter Ses- sions. He (Mr. Mclntyre) was not quite prepared to take all appeals in ordinary rating cases out of the hands of Quarter Sessions. Mr. Linaker: asked whether it meant to substitute a special court of appeal for the Quarter Sessions ? Mr. Mclntyre said that was so. Mr. Linaker : Instead of f'alcing appeals to the Quar- ter Sessions you will take them to a special court of appeal ? The Chairman : That is so. Mr. Woodward seconded the adoption of the recom- mendation of the committee. In view of certain pro- ceedings that were engaging their attention just then, tbouribt they had a good object lesson that such a court of appeal was one that commended itself to the general approval of the community. fie thought they would have been in a very much better position to-day if such a court of.appeal was in existence. Mr. Lirtaker supported the motion. He could say from exnerience that the Quarter Sessions was not always the best court to take appeals to. In an appeal in which he was interested there was a gross mis-carriageof justice and he attributed it to a certain combination on the tribunal.
Mr. Woodvvard said h objected to the latter part of the resolution with regard to the report of the Royal Committee.
It was resolved to support the resolution or the Pree- cot Union with the exception referred to.

Mr. C. E. Linaker, proposed the adoption of the minutes of the Frodsham Parochial, Committee. TUNED R AN ISOLATION HOSPITAL.

Mr. F. J. Walmsley, secretary of the Chester Isolation Hospital, wrote intimating that the Institution had been opened for the reception of infectious cases. and that in accordance with his communication of the 22nd August, 1896, such patients would no longer be received at the Infirmary. The Clerk intimated he had also an account from the same institution for tha maintenance ef Albert Corker. Amelia Corker, and Ernest Corker in the Infirmary at £2 per week-239 6s ; and fee for nuraes £1 16s id. The patients were admitted in accordance with resolutions passed empowering Mr. Moseley Williams and the Medical Officer to do what was necessary. The accounts would of course require the sanction of the Local Govern- ment Board and the point to him appeared to be what would the Local Government Board say when the accounts came before them.
Dr. Adams: If I remember rightly you were threatened with surcharge. The Clerk continuing : The Local Government Board will want to know our position with ragard to the Isolation Hospital.

Mr. Moseley Williams said they would probably remember the case, Mr. Kydd, himself and he thought Mr. Linaker and the medical officers were authorised to do what was necessary. It was found advisable to send the people away and it was only after very great per- severance that they were eventually got into Chester. In concluding Mr. Williams added that it only pointed to the want of some arrangement on the part of the Council to aeree with some suitable institution for the reception of such patients. Mr. S. Woodward asked whether they were to under- stand that those were the customary charges made in such hospitals. Dr. Adams referred to the arrangements made by the Warrington Corp)ration whose contract price for such eases was £2 2. per week. Ho believed it to be the customary_ charge. •
The Chairman: Of course our clerk can enquire. On the proposition of Mr. M. Williams it was decided tl pay the account.
LIGHT RAILWAY FROM WARRINGTON TO RUNCORN

Messrs. Bennett and Ward consulting and -efe3trical engineers, 13. Victoria Buildings, Manchester. wrote, under date, November 27h, as follows: —"lt is proposed to seek powers under the Light Railways Act to con- struct a light railw iy from Warrington to Runcorn pass- ing through your district as per enclosed ordnance sheet. We would like to receive your sup oort in promoting this bil by a formal resolution passed on your board by certifying that you are in favour of the scheme. By the line marked on the plan, we have kept by the road, and we prefer tr) do where possible in order that passengers can be taken up and set down in the usual way. The system would be the Electrical Trolly System, similar to that iw vogue at Liverpeel, Leeds, and other places ; the guaee would be 4ft. Bhin., and the speed would be limitel to 8 miles an hour. Under the Light Railways Act the proposed company would have the right to convey goods and merchandise, which would be accomplished when re- quired by means of a trailing car attached to the pas- senger car, and this traffic could be dealt with during the night. Our Mr. Bennett will be glad to meet a com- mitte . of the various Councils concerned on the route." The matter was referred to the Parliamentary Com- mittee for consideration, and it was suggested that the deputation should be asked to confer with the com- mittee.

hat young church which had all that trouble and orrow cast upon them. and finally apprated to them all o double their subscriptions to the Mission and that hey would dive out of the hearts full of the love of the Lord Jesus Christ. (Applause.) The Rev. Marshall Hartley, who was more than cordi- ally received, in the course of an exceedingly able ad- dress, said he would therefore as rapidly and succinctly as possible, give them some of his experiences and impressions of the'work and workers of the missien field. He had been and seen the grace of God in the people, that was his experience, and he was glad that he had seen it, and he had exhorted other nations to become Christians. (Applause). He had not come there to tell them that they lasci saved their brethren and were to sing the psaln of victory. It was not so. The work accomplished was of eeurse a great one, but at present it was simply s thread, or a thin long rivulet, in the midst of a Harare or great desert of evil. He had net come to tell them that all their Christian converts were all absolutely perfect. That they knew was not even the case in England where, with all their sense of civilisation, they were conscieui of many defects. There- fore, it was not to be expected that the converts would be all they ceuld desire. Having referred to the manner in which even in England old supersititions died hard; he said it was small wonder that their converts had seme slight portion of their old superstitions clinging to them. He spoke highly of the different sects of mis- sionaries, and of the way they co-operated together for rood in the foreign mission field. Indeed, the mission field was the greatest of all evangelisers. (Hear, hear.) Speaking with especial reference to the work of the missionary amongst the Chinese, he testified to having sat and listened to them giving their testimony, and had heard their native preachers, and though he could not thoroughly understand all that was said, save through an interpreter, yet he had heard the true ring in what was said. (Hear, hear.) Henry Ward Beeches, bad said that some people "Prayed cream and lived skimmed milk "—(tanghter)—but he had found there was very little of that about the con- verted Chinese. (Applause.) There were people who had literally lost all things, and were alienated and counted as dead by their relatives because they had gone over to Cnrist, but they were happy in it, and made joy out of their sufferings in the great joy of the Lord. (Applause.) He had seen the convert coming up and laying down his idol at the feet of tSe mi:sionary in token that he required it no more. He had seen in the faces of chinamen—in the most repulsive of faces—with their slit-eyes. their dull and heavy leer, their bridgeless noses, and yellow skins, the shiny hairless head with the inevitable pigtail— faces that were repulsive and would frighten to look upon—he had seen them lighted ,up with a light that was never kindled by any human power whatever—the light of the love of the Lord Jesus Christ. (Applause.) The substance of his message to those people, most of whom he had only seen once, was to cleave unto the Lord steadfastly. In his journey. legs he came to recognise one word that dominate.] in their worship. He could not under- stand all they said but he recognised the native word for " Christ " and came to listen for it with a pleasure and a joy that had given the worJs " How sweet the name of Jesus sounds in a believer's ear "an entirely new meaning to him. (Hear, hear.) The Chinese had no music in their souls, and he characterised their efforts to sing as the beating of tin trays, intermingled with the schereltsoy's " cat call " and the most discordant noises possible, all beine accompanied by the most astounding gronaces. (Laughter.) Yet it was delightful to find that even that unmusical people when they got religion got the desire to Ging. Touchine upon th adminis- tration, the rev. speaker said the Chinese were taught to build their own "Jesus house," and they had an amusinse., way of doing so. The people were locked in the room and none allowed to go until they had given or promised to give some- thing. Nor was that all, tbe sums promised ,were read out an] then some one woeld get up and say who could afford to give more. (Laughter.) The speaker then dealt with Ceylon and the Mission at Hyderabad, and spoke of the power that education was aiving them for the convertion of the nations. There was no conscience clause there and the people recognising the value of education sent their children to school woere they were taught the rudiments of Christianity. (Hear, hear.) In concluding Mr. Hartley referred to the great desire the people had for the Gospel, and their one cry seemed to be " why don't yeti send a teseher to us" had impressed upon his hearers the necessity of doing their utmost to further the work. 0 i resuming his seat after an hour and a quarter's spsech Mr. Hartley was loudly ap- plauded, Major General Campbell, at the Chairman's request, then contributed several native lvricsand hymns. Mr. T. &mister proposed and Mr. G.Bellarny seconded a hearty vote of thanlts to the Chairman and deputation which was heartily accorded. The collection for the evening reachel £22, and the meeting concluded after the Beeedietion was pronounced by the Rev. C. W. L Christien.

DEATH AND FUNERAL OF MRS. JOHN DAVIES. It was with deep regret that the intelligence reached Runcorn of the death of Mrs. Mary Davits, wife of Cap- tain John D ivi, s, of the steamship " Skirmisher " (Cunnard tender), and of 33, Burleigh-roid, North Everton, which took place on Friday last, after a leng and painful illness, at her residence. Deceased was a native of Runcorn, and general sympathy was expressed on all hands for the loss Captain Davies, sustains thiough the removal of his life's partner.—The funeral toek place at the Rencora Cemetery, on Tuesday last, and was largely attended. Mods were drawn along the route takeu by the funeral cortege and other manifes- tations of sympathetic regret were visible on all hands The body was removed to Runcorn by road but the procession W 49 formed at the Runcorn Station whither the Liverpool friends and relatives of the eceased journeyed by train. The pre- cession included the following meurners and a number of other friends :—Captain John Davies (husband). Mrs Buchanan. Mr and Mrs Hughes, and two sons (Liverpool). Mr T Bittern, and miss C Hilton, (Runcorn). Mr and Mrs J H and Mr E Lea (Widnes),Mr. and Mrs. T Davies (brother-in-law) Mr G H Davies, Mrs G H Davies, Mr W Davies, Mr T Davies (jun), Mr and . Mrs J W (Widno.), Mr and Mrs J Davies, Mr and Mrs T Davies,Mr and Mrs Joseph Banner (Runcorn), Mrs Jaegers (Liverpeol). Mrs James Corker (Runcorn), Mr W Banner, Mr Georgs Burner, Mr T Banner, Mr R A Banner, Mrs James Edwards, Mrs J Ornae, Mrs Maddock and two daughters (Runenro). Mrs Blower (New Brighton). Miss M -J Cotterall (Liverpool), Mrs Bebbington, Mrs W Leathwoad (Runcoro), Captains Edwarl and Richard Davies (friends) (Runcorn). At the Cemetery the burial service was conducted by the Rev %V Biker, of Liverpool (Bielinp of the Reformed Chwrch of England), who also gave an address to the female b.fore leaving the Church. After the funeral the party. adjourned to the Guild Hall, St. Johe-street, Runcorn, where tea was provided.

div.head: Annual Meeting at St. Paul's Church, Runcorn. Handsome Collections.
div.p: Annual Meeting at St. Paul's Church, Runcorn. Handsome Collections.

In connection with the furthering of the work of the Wesleyan Foreign Missionary Socie:y,suecessful services were held in St. Paul's Chapel, on Sunday Jas.:, and the annual meeting on Monday night, was also conducted at the same p!ace. The Rev. Marshall Hartley.of (London), secretary of the C)aference, aril one of the general secretaries at the Mission House, London, and Major General Campbell, late of Her Mije,ty's Forces in Hyderabad. India, were the deputation from the parent Society, and delivered elownt serrnens and addresses to large congregations. The collec:ions thraug,hout totalled £l6O 163 3d,

On Sunday morning the Rev. Marshall Hartley founded his discourse upon " He saved others ; himself he cannot save" Matt. xxvii, 42, and drew oPautiful lessons from his text illustrative of the sacrifices thar, were of necessity to be made for the accomolishing of successful missions. In the evening the preacher chose for his subject "He first findeth his own brother, and brought him to Jesus." St. John I. 41 and 42 and exhorted his hearers to firs: find their own brothers—to work amongst their own cauntrymen and women, but not to stop there. In the afternoon Major General Camp- bell addressed the scholars attending the Brunswick Schools upon the mission work at Hyderabad, and sang several native hymns for the edification of his hearers. He referral also, in glowing terms, to the value of the work accomplished by the younger members of the school as collectors, and encouraged them to greater efforts in so noble a cause.

The annual meeting was held at St Paul's On Monday evening, and considering the steady downpour of rain which fell incessantly during the latter portion of the day, a satisfactorily large attendance assembled under the chairmanship of Mr. A. R. Norman, J.P. Support- ing him on the platform were the R“v Marshall Hartley, Major-General Campbell, Revs C W L Christien (aesis- tent superintendent), Humphreys, Morrison, W Fidoe, Messrs F J Norman, J.P., R H omet, E Taylor (secretary), G Bellamy (treasurer), T Sirnister, Samuel Taylor, J.P., H Moston (Frodsham), T Boote and others. After devotional exerci!e by the Rev C W L Christien, and the singing of a suitable hymn The Rev. H. Morrison submitted the report of the Parent Society. Having dealt with the general scope of the mi.sion work, he referred to the fact that last year the society had sent out foureen additional missionaries. It was gratifying also to see that last year there had been an increase in the funds of thesociety of some £l,lOO, and not only had there been a mere increase on the past year, but that increase Came upon what he believed to be a steady increase for two or three years previously. (Applause.) It was pleasing to see that rising tide of generosity on the part of their people towards that work. (Hear, hear.) Tney were further told there had been an increase in tee member- ship on the mission field, and though they knew very well they could not estimate the inerease in toe sp:rit of Jesus among the nations of the world, yet thy prayed that that might be correspondingly great. (Applause.) The income for the last year was £130,533, but there was simply one item in that to which he would refer, viz., the amount raised year by year by 'their young people. -The amount their young people raised last year alone was £30,000. (Applause.) He felt that any cause that touched the hearts and enthusiasm of the young people, as was evident that cause did, was certain of intimate success. (Applause.) They had on the mission field 309 European missionaries, and a membership in their mission churches of 46,000, and they bad in the schools about 90.000 scholars. (MAN hear.) He would add one local sentence in conclusion whion was expres- sive sf the pride he felt in belonging to a ercuit whieh most especially through its young people VIVI doing so much and working so earnestly to extend the Kingd srn of the Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ. (Applause.) Mr E Taylor (local secretiry) then submitted the local reports, from which it appeared that uo to that rneetinC.' the total amount collected reached £l2B lie 91, made up as follows :—Collectei by Mrs S rulby. £1 is; Mrs E Marshall, £3 9s 6d : Mrs P Booth, £3 2s 61 ; Mrs Bellamy. £6 16s 61 ; Miss Norman, £9 is ; Miss Doris May Posnett, £9 N6l ; Sunday collections £l5 2s 01; Sunday Schools, £BO 18i 9 I.—The Woman's auxiliary also contributed £lO 4s 6 I.—The collection for that evening he would announce later.

The Clairman said as regarded the interest ofßuncorn in the Wesleyan Foreign Mission, he thought tee report which had just been read sys reply enough—(hear, hear)—and for a reply to the Quaker question' As to how much they were in sympatny with the cause " they had nothing to do but point to those fimres—(loul applause.) Nor was that all for in the Runcorn Circuit he was proud to say they did not stick at raising money. They had also provided missionaries (renewed applause.) He referred especially to the Rev Samuel Ravenscroft, who laboured so succesSfully in South Africa, to Mr. Summerville, and the noble way in which be ,leal sacrificed his life in the =ashen course, dying' a premature death, and also to the Rev C Posnett, and his sister. (Applause.) Although Mr. Posnett and his sister had not actually proceeded out of Runcorn. they coeld not help but feel a very close relatiocship to him throe:4h his brother Mr Robert Posnett. (Hear, hear.) Major General Cemphol', who was most cordially re- ceived, described his feeliegs to be akin to those fait by a native he once met in India, awl who in answer te a query as to who he w ?s r p'ird " A volnnteer by f oree." (Laughter.) He had been written to by hie friend Mr. Robert Posnett, and asked whether he would come up and address the children at the schoo7s on the Sunday afternoon. Naturally he replied that he would be de- lighted. But on arrival at Runeern a progTemme was put into his hands, and he forme that he was one of the speakers for that meeting. (Renewed lauehter ) Be was glad to be present, however, and to look epoa the faces of his fellow country men and women in that chapel who were showing their sympathy with the work of the salvation of the souls of black people out in India. (Hear, hear.) They told him, and he had heard men say, that the natives were not worth caring for. He had heard men despise the natives; and he had heard men talk of the native christians as if they were the scum of the earth—(diame)—and as if they bad no hearts. That was because they die not know them. They had hearts like their own—(hear, hear) —and he for one would never forget the personal love he had received from a native, when he was in great distress, and had lost everything It was the iove of a native that had sav4cl him. (Ap- plause.) Did not that prove a heart—(hear, hear).— and were nut such people worth savine. (Applause ) In conclusion the speaker referred to the mission at Ryder-, abad where he had been stationed and where his friend' —whom he could never foreet—Charlie Posnett, and hie young sister, were working for Christ. He had received a letter—a most pathetic letter—from Mr. Posnett, in which he told him of a terrible famine that was upon them, and his heart went out to them. He could think of those two faithful people as they sat surrounded by a number of natives stricken with the terrible plague and stretching•forth their heed: askine for bread. He IVe. sure that Charlie Posnett would eive them all he had bx.lr. even that would not deliver them from the tprrihl, scourge of the country. He hoped they would pray for
