div.head: BEFORE the MAGISTRATES
div.p: BEFORE the MAGISTRATES

A WOMAN'S IMPUDENT THEFT.—SAD CASE. At the Warrington Beroueh Police Court on Saturday, before Messrs Birchall (in the their), J. W. Hayward. and R. T. Fairciough, Margaret Ann Appleton, 46,Willis- street, was charged with stealing frena a drawer in the bedroom of the dwelling house 28, Willis-street some- time between the 21st and 22nd of October, £6 5s in cash, several articles of jewellery, a number of old coins and some trinkets, the property of Police-Sergeant Lawrence.—She was further charged with being a suspicious person and being found under the bed in the house of Peter Faulkner, Gorsey-lane.—She pleaded guilty.—The Chief Coestable stated the facts of the case at some length. He said that Sergeant Lawrence was a =ember of the police force employed at the forgeoend his wife kept a shop in Willis-street off Gorsey-la,ne. Prisoner lived close by and appeared to be a respectable young married woman. Her husband was a fitter in the employ of the Cheshire Lines Committee, and she had absolutely I no reason for resorting to criminal habits. She seemed, however, to have taken to them not with the instincts of a novice, but with the experience of an expert. 'On Saturear, the 21st of October, Mr. Lawrence saw his cash which amounted to £6 53. in gold and silver safe in a canvas bag in the drawer of a dressing table in his bedroom, and on the same date the jewellery and old coins were seen safe in the drawer of a dressing table in the bedroom of Mr. Lawrence's daughter. On the following morning at eight o'clock the drawer in Mr. Lawrence's room was found to be prized open and the contents had been abstracted. It was also discovered' that true trinkets and coins in the other room had been Wren, and the box in which they were kept thrown on one • side. They were at an absolute loss to know how the nines had gone as there was absolutely no means by which the prisoner could have possessed herself of the things than by walking boldly through the shop in the day time, going upstairs and taking them whilst Mr. Lawrence was in bed. It had transpired from her own confession that she did that. The police were informed of the occurrence and inquiries were made. Strong suspicion was attached to the woman because she was a customer of Mrs. Lawrence and had frequently seen Mrs. Law- rence go upstairs for change. It was also ascertained by the police that the women was spending money pretty freely and was paying her debts. The paid one hong standing debt that she owed to Sergeant Lawrence. She did other things that showed she had had a windfall in same way ter other. Suspicion did not amount to proof and no steps were t Ikea, the woman's position being of such respectability that she was not arrested. Another woman named Faulkner kept a shop in the neighbourhood, wad prisoner dealt with her and kaew that she kept her money upstairs. She had about £8 upstairs. At 5 o'clock on Thursday last, Mrs. Faulkner left the house entirely unoccupied. She was sway about a quarter of an hour and when returning she was approaching the house and saw through the window someone going upstairs with a light. She was very much astonished so she went in and at once went upstairs. There was no trace of a light, so she struck a light and was petrified to see a. boot poking Irons under the bed. A boot would have been harmless enough, but there was a foot in it. She was alarmed and came downstairs, and met a Mrs. Price coming into the shop. They went upstairs and met the prisoner coming down. Mrs. Faulkner said to b-r" Whatevrr are you here for ? You frightened me dreadfully." The prisoner replied that a great tall man ran after her and she went into the house to get out of his way. This invention did not satisfy the woman and information was given to the police. Superintendent Monaghan and Detective Dela- bay visited the prisoner's house and told her she was strongly suspected of going to a house for an unlawful purpose. She repeated the story about the man pursu- ing her. Superintendent Monaghan was not satisfied and told her that she was suspected of committing the robberfat the hence of Sergeant Lawreace. She stoutly denied the offence for some time but she subsequently admitted it and said she did not know *hat made her do it. She produced a pawnticket for one of the stolen articles which had been sold for 4s 6d. It was one of the most extraordinary canes he thought that had ever come before the court.—Prisoner's husband was called and said that his wife repeatedly pawned his things. Oa one occasion she had pawned his watch and chain.— The Chief Constable said the police found some pawn- tickets up the chineney.—Prisaner had nothing to say.— The Chairman said it was one ef the strangest cases he had ever heard. It was prisoners first offqnce and that stood somewhat in her favour. She would have to go to peison 'for two months with hard labour and they hoped it would be a lesson to her.

He said the woman was found endeavouring to get ever the railings near Arpley to get into the river and was announcing very emphaticelly that she Intended to do away with herself as she was tired of life Her eonduct attracted the attention of PS. Lewis, and after a struggle with her he got her to the Police Station. Prisoner appeared to have been in drink for some time. and be (the Chief Constable) asked for a remand for a week, in order that she might go to gaol and ' got the drink out of her."—The remand Was granted. • ALLEGED ASSAULTS. —CASES DIBMVISED. --TIIOIPaS Gal!Op, 21, Hopwood-street. was summoned for Reasoning Mary Griffiths. 2, Eldon-street on the 27th November. —Nathan Griffiths, husband of the complainant Mary Griffiths. was summoned for assaulting Hannah Jolley. 47. school-brow, on the same date.—Mr. A Browne appeared for the complainant Mrs. Griffiths. He said that she kept a shop at the corner of Eldon-street and School-brow. On Monday night the woman Hannah Jolley went into the shop between eight and nine o'clock. Mr Griffiths was serving behind the counter as his wife was out, and he served the woman with a quantity of provisions. Fairciough • FOUR MONTHS TOR ASsAIILTING THE PoLICE —jamas Leonardy, Silver-street, was charged with being drunk and disorderly in Win "43k-street at 11-55 the previous night and with assaulting P.C.'s Clough and Turner.—P.o, Clough said that at the time in question he was on duty in plain clothes in company with P O. Turner going in the direction of the "Lord Rodney "public house, when prisoner came up to him and tried to put hi'. is oc.l in his overcoat pocket. Witness resisted and asked him what he wanted. Be replied "Oh, I thought it was my brother Joe." Witness remons- trated with him and he struck him on the left side. P.O. Tamer then came up and they tried to secure the man. He was very violent and threw himself to the ground. and kicked, and struck out in all directions. He kicked P.O. Turner on the left hand and struck him several times about the body. They had several struggles on the ground on the way to the Police Station.— P.O. Turner corroborate I. :---Prisoner denied the offence, and produced a summons ordering him to join the Militia.— the Chief Constable said that men seemed to think that if they had anything to do with a red-coat they should be discharged for any offence up to wilful murder. —Prisoner had been before the Court twenty-two times and was one of the roughest and worst characters in the town.—Prisoner was committed to gaol for four months with hard labour. A BICYCLE THEFT.—George Brown, of no fixed address was ch.rged with stealing from the "Eagle and Child" Yard, Bridge-street, a safety bicycle value £lB 10s.. the pro- perty of Richard Wright—He pleaded guilty—The Chief Oanstable said the prisoner was before the Magistrates on Monday, charged with being drunk and disorderly, and it was then intimated that a charge of stealing a bicycle would probably be made against him. It app.ared that on the evening in question. Mr. Richard Wright, who was the son of Mr. Joseph Wright, of Great Sankey, had cause to go to the" Eagle and Child" Inn, on business. He left t.,e bicycle, which was a new one and had only been ridden two or three times, in the yard. Before geing .nto the public- house he noticed the prisoner hinging abut the yard. the next that was seen of the prisone, was when he was ob- served by P.O. Newey in Golborn -street at 8.20 wheeling the bicycle. The constable thought it unlikely that the machine would belong to him std accosted him. Prisoner ran the bicycle against the wall and stood away from it and said" I have no bicycle. I have nothing to do with the bicycle." Ho was taken into custody and he said "If I had been able to.ride it you would not have caught me this night." In order that he (the Chief Constable) might make inquiries he was only charged with drunkenness on Monday His inquiries were now complete and he left the case in the hands of the Bench.—Prisoner was sent to gaol for two months with hard labour.

A GIRL'S RELYCTANT CROlCE.—Blizabeth Ann Martin, 18 years of aze, whom, it will be rememberel was remanded frdna the last court, so that efforts could be made by the police to get her into some kind of a home,was again brought up; the charges azainst her were two for larceny.—The Superintendent of Police intimated he wolVd withdraw the charges against the girl upon her consenting to go to the home that Miss Wright. of Chester. would provide for her.— Prisoner said she would go for a period of 6or 9 months. The Clerk pointed out, that such a time would be to little, as Miss Wright state 4. the girl would most likely at the end of that time be no better and when outside the influence of the home would do the same thing again. —The Chairman told prisoner she would have to be dealt with by them,where- upon she consented to go with Miss Wright for as long as necessary.—The charges were withdrawn and prisoner dis- missed.

SERIOUS ASSLULT CLIEC.—A. FOOTBALLER IN TROUBLE.— James Weston, carpenter's apprentice, 33,11:1i0n-street, Run- corn, was OOMMOoId by Ohtries Clucas, carpenter's appren- tice for assault on the 12th of November.—Mr. Knowles, solicitor. Widnes, prosecuted, and Mr. F. A. Lake, solicitor, Runcorn, appsarei for the defence. —Mr Knowles said it would appear that the complainant was with another boy named Gregory on the 12th of November, 'when the defendant who " had it in for them" sl mead Gregory and canght hold of Gimes by the throat, nearly strangled him and than threw him violently to the ground lareakine his collar bone. The boy was picked up by Gregery, and was subsequently attended by Dr. McLennan.—ln support of this statement Charles Clucas,l6 years of age, the complainant ; Walter Gregory, Wellington- itreet ; Edward Brassendale ; and Fenny g!lueas, (complain- ant's mother), were called.—Dr. McLennan testified to the nature of the injuries. Clucas was eximined by him and found to be sufferlng from a simple fracture of the collar bone. He was suffering great pale and there was a large swelling which gave him some diffieulty in locating the fracture.—Mr A F Lake, for the defence, admitted causing the injury. He, 'aewever, allufed to what had led up to the assault. The bays Clucas and Grego-y bad caused Weston considerable annoyessee by whistling after him and causing him to turn round for nothing. Previous to the 12th November they had some werds about it. and Weston had been threatened " that if he touched oni he w..uld have to touch the two." Meeting them on the 12th he had gone and asked Gregory what he meant b 7 what he said the previous Sunday Clucas evidently came up to assist his mate, and Weston shoved him off with the result that he fell and the injury was caused. He contended that his client was justified in defending himself from the threatened attack of Owes: He also intimated that the defendant was very generously disposed and bad offered to pay the doctor's hid when he heard that Clucas was so seriously injured by his fall—His was substantiated by the defendant ; James Whatcroft ; Harold Dunbaviu and Fred Davies. The Chairman said they considered there was no doubt about the assault, which was a most serious one Weston would have imposed upon him the fell penalty £5, or one months' imprisonment. The fine included £4 3s costs.

The Mayor of Leigh kictr,d off,Fairhurst returnirg. A mull by Pe irsoei gave Warrington a footing in the Leigh half. Bate threw to Isherwood who broke away with Fish in attendance and a try should have followed, but the centre hold too long and was tackled near the line. Warrington carried the first scrimmage and Bats tried to get over, but being tackled he parted to Taylor who scored eavily near the corner. Warrington's early success was received with cheers by their supporters. Jones made an excellent attempt at goal. Leigh cleared by the aid of a free kick which was mulled by Smith, and Molyneux and Davies gained further ground. Duckworth promptly upset the latter before he had travelled far. Fine followiei •up by War- rington put them on the attack once more, Merryweather grassing Winstauley at the centre. Duckworth distin- guished himself by a clever dribble fro:rattle scrummage to the home 25 where Pearsen saved. Davies took ad- vantage of a mull by Jones, but was stnartly upset b r Smith. All Leigh's attempts at combination were swiftly nipped in the bud. Warring- ton contributed a beautiful passing run,Fish just failing to round Davies. More nice combination by the War- rington backs preyed too much for Leigh. Smith fed Jones very cleverly but the wing man found Winstanley an awkward obstacle after making geod runs. Bate charged a kick dawn and Smith dashed over the line with the ball, but a knock on spoiled a clever try. The Leigh custodian was given plenty t 3 do and had to touch down before Isherwood and Fish. Molyneux created a diversion by dodging nicely away from the scrimmage and passed to Cildicott. The latter dashed off down toueh but was bowled over by Fish in War- rington territory. Davies did good work, and Molyneux had a fruitless drop at goal. Leigh returned to the attack with spirit and Winstan- ley marked near the Warrington goal. He essayed a drop and had hard hick the ball passing under the bar. Leigh managed a bout of passing, Ganley seeming to have a chance but Jon's tackled strongly. Molyneux punted' from touch and Warrington failing to reply the Leigh front rank rushed the ball ever the line and Boardman scored amid great cheering. Molyneux failed at goal, and the interval arrived with the sore, a try each.

Taylor resumed,Leigh sending into touch. Fish put in a nice kick whieh gave Warrington the upper hand. Nice passing gave Jonas a chance to run down the touch line and then centre. Merry weather secured, and made a de- tnanined effert to get over the line. Jones had a grand chance given him by Duckworth,but missed the pass. Play had hardly resumed before Duckworth was off in the opposite direction, and passing nicely to Isherwood the latter f.d Fish, who scared neatly at the corner. Jones failed at goal. Exciting play foliewed, the home team straining every nerve to draw level again. Pearson smartly intercepted a pass and kicking over the line,gave Caldicott a chance which was promptly taken, the cheering being terrific. Molyneux kicked a goal,but the whistle having eoancled he had to t ike the kick again and failed. If possible play became faster and more ex- citing then ever. Warriagton got pessession and Isher- wood punted to the line, where Winstanley made an error of kith:meat and was tackled. Pearson attempted to kick eleer, but Fish caeght the ball and electrified everybody by sprinting in again at the corner. Jones was again unsuceessfal ttioeeh he malts a good attempt at goal. Warrington once more held the lead and strove hard to maintain it. They were very smart and 'held Leigh in cheek. Jones should have added to the score but again missed Duck worth's pass at the corner. Fish got over at the other aide a moment later but had been in tench al(' Leigh breathed freely once more. They were su*cteti to a hot attack,Davies marking on the line and affording some relief. Molyneux sent play to the other end where BISCOW touched down judiciously. Jones mulled several cstele6s and Warrington began to have an :Anxious time. Isherwood. Smith, and Boscow were practically cafe, h wever, and Leigh were continu- ally sent 13t2it. Merry weather once more grassed Win- ataniny, and some hot work followed. Dackworth,Snaith and Jones passed well but failed to get threugh. Merry- weather got the ball and throwing wide to Fish the latter nenpluied the Leighites by racing in for the third time and grounding behind the posts. Jones kicked a geal. Leigh made one more effort hut were repelled by Bos- cow,and the end came with the score reading : Warring ton, 1 goal 4 tries (14 points) ; Leigh, 2 tries (6 po hits)

THE EXAMINER, FRIDAY, DECEMBER 8, 1899.
Huddersfield v. Liversedge.

At Huddersfield, where this match was played, the borne fifteen gained a well-merited victory by two tries (obtained by Jenkins and Smith) to one penalty-goal (kicked by Todhill). Hunslet v. Wakefield Trinity.
The Trinitarians entertained flutislet, a hall they de- feated by two zoals and twa triei to a aoal and a try. Lockwood, M- tcalfe,A Gildthorpe and Bradburn scored for their respective sides.

No scoring took place in this match at Halifax till the second half, when the superior play of the home players asserted itself, and they left the field winners by a goal ana two tries to nil.
Brighouse Rangers v. Holbeck.
These teams were se evenly matched at Brighouse that neither side could gain any tangible advantage, the result being a pointless draw. Castleford v. Brarnley.
The home combination had the advantage in this game at Castleford. and won by three trie3—obtained by Holland. Speed, and Salmon, after some brilliant pass- ing—to nil. Batley v. Bradford.
A stiff fight was witneesA at Batley, where the:home team managed to wrest a victory from theft powerful opponents by a goal and a try to nil.
Warrington " A " v. Leigh "A."

These teams met on the Wilderspool enclosure on Saturday afternoon, and the home fifteen once again asserted their superiority. Mason was unable to play but a representative team was placed in the field and the three-quarter line composed of Moores, Holcroft, Ratcliffe and Howard was especially prominent. It was encouraging to see such a largo attendance, and the col- lection taken up on behalf of the Mayor's fund must have realised a satisfactory sum. The Borough Band enlivened the proceedings with a number of selections and the members indulged in a march round the field at half time. Leigh kicked off but were ordered back for off side play and a scrimmage took place on the line. Bate ietercepted a pass and threw across to Ratcliffe who made considerable progress into the visitors twenty-five. The pressure was continued for some time, and then a misfortune befel the Leigh team, one of the forwards receiving such injury that he had to be carried off the field. The game was resumed, but the visitcrs played only fourteen mee throughout the game. A pretty pasaieg movement between Ratcliffe and Howard almost resulted in the latter scoring. Shortly af erwarcls Andrews took advantage of some fumbling on the line by the Leigh hacks, and thus opened Warrington's Fcering account. Holctoft failed at the goal kick Moors was next prominent, and scored an unimproved try from a pass by Holcroft. The home team were now having most of the game and Moores caused a round of applause by a tricky run through the thick of his opernents and completing the effort by a capital try. Jolley on this occasion tried to increase the points but missrabiy failed. Half-time arrived with the home team leading by three tries to nil. In the second half Leigh were completely outclassed and rarely had a look in. Moores scored his third try of the match after a fine run. The fiith and last try was planted beyond the magic line by Holcroft and:Warrington ran out whiners by nye tries (15 points) t ) Leigh nil.

COUNTY CHAMPIONSHIP. Lancashire Defeat Cheshire.

This important match took place at winton, in the presence of 10,000 spectators. Lancashire attacked strongly at the start, and Lawton obtained a try after clever passing, but Frater failed at gnat: Afterwards give-and-take play ensued, both sides attacking in turn, but without result. Towards the interval Lancashire again assumed the upper hand, Williams getting a try. Half-time—Lancashire, 2 triAs (6 paints); Cheshire, nil. On resuming Lancashire attacked strongly, Lees almost scoring after a couple of brilliant dashes. Then Hadwen was within an ace of placing a goal, but the Cheshire defence was brilliant in the extreme, and in the closing stages the visitors' forwards were dangerous with their clever footwork and rushes. Nothing further was scored, and Lancashire won the championship. Result—Lanca- shire, 2 tries (6 points) ; Cheshire, nil. LANCASHIRE SENIOR COMPETITION. -- Fine Performance by Warrington.

The return match between Warrington and Leigh came off at Leigh on Saturday, and resulted in favour of Warrington by 1 goal 4 tries (14 paints) to Leigh 2 trios (6 points). Warrington went ta Leigh with the determination to win it possible and they succeeded in a fashion which passed all anticipation. Smith, late of Wigan, appeared in thç centre for Warringtou, who were at full strength. lLsigh laeked the services of Dunbavin and W. Roberts, but had substitutes in An- derton and Greenhalgh. Mr. lkyeutcheon (Oldham)was the referee and be had the teams well in hand all through. The weather was ideal for the game, and the ground being in good order nlay was of a fast deecrip- tion. There were about 5.000 spectators present,includ- ing the Mayor of Leigh (Alderman J. Fairclnugh) and a number of councillors and ladies. Two bands played martial music and a collection was taken in aid of the Re- servists. etc. The teams were composed as folluws

Warrington : Boscow, full back; Fish, Isherwood, Smith and Jones, tbreequarters ; J T Bate and Duck- worth, half backs: Tayior, Morrison, Boardman, Merry- weather, Eden, Swift, Scholtze and Fairhurst,forwards. Leigh: Winstanley, full back, Oaldicott, Pearson Davies, and Ganley, three quarters; Molyneux and Anderton, half-backs; Smith, J Roberts, Greenhalgh, McMasters, Taylor, Boardman, Collins, and Eccleston, forwards.

Warrington v. Tranmere Rovers.

Plgyed at Warrnagtou on Saturday afternoon. War- rington won the toss and Hancock started for the visit tors. An attack followed, Murray spoiling the effort. Tranmere broke away, but Mather obtained possession and centred in good position, Pierpoint heading a goal for Warrington. Two corners followed for tile home team without success. Warrington maintained the attack, but Taylor shot wide. Aepinall was called upon to save from Doyle. Warrington returned to the attack but were penalised in a favourable position. Pierpoint shot well, and Williams gave a corner in saving. The visitors failed to make any headway, and severe. corners fell to Warrington without tangible result Robertson effected A clever save tram Pierpoint, and for a brief period the Tranmere goal was thoroughly bom- barded. Lea was respansible in checking a rush by Warrington, and a fruitless corner resulted. Half-time— Warrington one, Trannaere nil. Play during a great portion of the second half 'was of a give-and-take nature, but near the close the Warringtanians attacked strongly and the outcome of some smart play by Riley and Hackett saw Pierpoint score a second goal, Warrington thus winning by two goals to nil. LANCASHIRE LEAGUE. Earlestown v. Chorley.

Earlestown appearoi on the Mearine enclosure on Saturday to play off their first match with last year's champions of the Lancashire League. Earlestown played the same team as that which drew with Wigan County last week, with one excrption, Whitehouse fail- ing to put in an appearance, ane Pennington taking his place. Cherie? were also without one or two of their regular players, but very capable reserves filled the vacant positions. The following were the teams.:— Earlestewn : Chew, goal ; Hayes and Cottem, hacks ; Green. Parr, and Johnson, halt backs ; Linton, Penning- ton, Hamoson, Leach and Settle, forwards. Chorley : Pennington. goal; Thoruber and Green. backs ; Mitchell, D)cleirtv and Morton, "half backs ; Po ley Swarebrick, Cunliffe, Lord, and Aston, forwarie. The visitors arrived late, and it was three o'clock before a start was mede. Chew won thee:toss, and he elected to play aezainst the slope, Cuntiff3 setting the ball in motion on behalf of Chorley before ab )ut 1,000 spectators, anti in beautiful football weather. The opening exchanges were chiefly in favour of Earlestown, the left wing 'ii pair being early prominent. The visitors' custodian was the first to be called upon, a lovely shot from Settle bringing him to his knees. A clever piece of tackling by Green resulted in Linton obtaining possession. He raced away up the wing, and when well situated put in a fine centre which was met by Settle woo shot in hard. Pennington having to Con cede a corner to get the leather clear. This was success- fully negotiated and nice play by the Chorley left wine- transferred play to the other end. Here Lord gave Chew a warm handful, the custodian just tipping the leather over the bar. Toe ensuing carrier wes easily j cleared and the homesters were soaa hovering round j the Chorley goal aertin. A foul close in against the visi- tors lo")ked ominous for them but ?err nullified a glori- oue chance by shooting pada over the bat. A nice run along the line by Lord was followed by a grand centre but Sevarsbrick, who met the ball, shot the wrong side of the post. Pretty passing by the home forward) followed and Flempson was left with a maguifient opening. He shot in bard and straight and Peunington caueht the ball but dropped it again. Thorn- ben however cleared the danger and play was eventually transferred to the horne goal, where Aston had hard lines in not scerine,. He obtained the ball at a difficult nnele and shot in at a terrific pace, Cnew bringing off a splendid save. At the interest it there was a clean sheet. RP-starting, Ceorley were the first to become dangerous Chew having to deal with shots from Aston and Cueliffe. From the latter's shot, the custodian had conceded a corner which was splendidly placed by Aiton, the bell glancing off the had of Parr on to the head cf S wars. brick and thus into the net. The had the effect of rousing the home team and they went at it with a will, one shot of Leach's deserving a better fate.Hewever.their efforts were at leneth rewarded, a lovely shot from Lin- ton from full 40 yards range beating Penniceton all to pieces. The shot was one of the best seen on the Memes ground for a long tirne,as Liuton was hampered by the Chotley half backs, but he turned round with mervellous rapidity and giving the ball a tap, he dodged the half hacks, pounoM on it egain,end—the scores were level, the (roster:lien falling in the attempt to save his charge. After this, the visitors were penned in their' own goal, and during a scrimmage on tha goal line, their custodian was badly mauled. No further scoring was done and the whistle blew with the score standing Ee.rlfstown one, Chorley one. Taking the game as a whole, a draw about represents the merits of the res- pective teams. It was abut as fast and exciting a vine as one could wish for, the pace being a cracker from the start

div.head: WARRINGTON AS A COUNTY BOROUGH.
div.p: WARRINGTON AS A COUNTY BOROUGH.
Memorial to the Local Government Board.

The Town Clerk on behalf of the Corporation has deposited a memorial with the Local Gos!ernment Board praying that IV4rrington be cone,ituted into a county borough. It is pointed out in the memorial that the area of the Baroult is 3,115 acres, and that the population, according to the census of 1891, was 52,742. The present population of the Borough is estimated by the Me,tical Officer of Health at 64,000. The population and rateable value of the Borough have rapidly increased, as is shown by the following figures _ .

The memorial also states that he Council are the owners of the Markets and of the Gas undertaking and the Water undertaking, and that they have obtained powers under the Warrington Electric Lighting Order of 1898,and are now erecting works for sapplying the Borough with Electric Light. The Council are also now applying to the Board of Trade for a provisional order to construct and work tramways within the Borough. The Council are also the owners of the following properties :—Town Hall, municipal offices, Parr Hell, Gymnasium, cemetery (30 acres), Bank Park (17i acres),Victoria Park (52 acres), Queen's Gardens (2 acres), Volun- teer quarters, Public Free Library, Museum and Art Gallery,sanitary depilt,two intercepting depOts, public bats, hospital for infectious diseases, public mortuary, fire brigade station, police station, stone and store yard, Schoal of Art, Technical Schools, two public wharves. The rateable value a the ad ministre tive county, including the Borough, is £22,957,661-, and the rateable value of the Borough on the °Linty rate basis is £227,632, the rateable value of the Borough for improvement rate being £204,531, and for the poor rate £222,465. The rates in the pound for county purposes levied within the Borough during the last three years have been as follows :-1897, 5J ; 1898. 4AI; 1899, 4d. Toe amount contributed by the Borough for county rates was :—For the year ended March, 1897, £3,394; 1898, £3,706; 1899, £3,612. The rates levied within the Borough dur- ing the last five years have been as follows :- 1895,53 10d; 1896, 5s 81; 1897, 6s 2d ; 1898, 6 1899, 6s.

The total liability of the Borough on the 31st March last, including the debt of the gas and water undertakings, end the capitalised value of the annuities cnarged on those undertakings, amounted to £589,271, made up as follows:—Borough rate, £30,023; improvement rate, £70,060; general sewers rate, £34,281; as undertaking, £183,792; water undertaking, £271,115. The total length of streets and roads within the borough is 39 miles, of wt:ich only 1 mile 6 furlongs are main roads. The Borough is watched by its own police, and receives out of moneys voted by Parliament one half of the Cost of the pay and clothing of the police. The Borough has received from the County Council, during the last five years. the following grants in aid of technical instruction, and the Borough has expended during the same period out of rates, the sum shown after the grant in each year : Year. Grant in Aid. Expended out of Rates. R. s. d. 2. e. d. 1894-5 910 0 0 1895-6 411 10 0 131 0 0 1898-7 334 0 8 208 13 2 1897-8 647 10 0 335 0 0 1893-9 553 10 0 335 0 0

In conclusion the memorialists respectfully re- present that having regard to the size and import- ance of the Borough, to the rapid increase of it population, to its geographinl poiition as regards the rest of the County, the best interests of the Borough would be served by its being constituted a County Borough, within the meaning of the Local Government Act, 1888.

div.head: MAN OF MARKS.
div.p: A MAN OF MARKS.
Chat with Mr. Walter Gibbs.

Circumstances have combined to mako Mr. Walter Gibbs a man of light and leading to his West-country neighbours. He resides at 9, EastbDurae-gate, Taunton, and is widely respected for his position and his shrowd,candid common-sense—conspicuous even among the hard-headed notables of that rAther " canny "dis- trict.

Mr. Gibbs, says the "Somerset County Express," from which the following interview h clipped, has a wife and five bright, happy young children. " I ,tin now thirty-two years cif age," said he, "and when in nay teens I worked for more than four yexes in a tan- yard, and had to carry heavy, wet loads. Since then— for over ten years—l have been in my present situation, in which I have charge of the shirt-starching depart- ment of the Somerset Manufacturing Company—work which necessitates my hands and arms being frequently in water."

" The water certainly seems to are with you," was the comment of the prase representative. " Yes; but do you see these marks on my taco, chin, and bands? I was always well till about three or four years ago, when ecz3ma apps red, and the marks you see are some of the oViderlC23 of what I suffered." " Please tell me how you were affi!cted."

"My legs, arms, flc2, and mast of nay body were covered with running, itching sores. I could not rest by day, and at night I was in soda incessant agony that I often felt inclined to throw myself out of the bc.,.;ircoaa window. I was completely laid up at times. At the kaee joints I had dreadful rheumatic pains, and my wife had to help ma upstairs. I put cloths on my arms, the' " wept "so much, and these clatha had to be changed every half-hour. I could not bear anyone to come near me, owing ta the fear I had that they would accidentally touch me. All my friends told me to try diff,n-ent reme- dies, but no good came of them. I had only one wish in life, and that was to die and be released from agony." What efforts, then, did you make to obtain a cure?" asked Use reporter. " I went as an in-patient to the hospital, and after treatment there, I was discharged as cured, but two months afterwards I was as bad as ever. I then W- came an out-patient for four months, but this was no good. I was next under a doctor for seven mouths, but appeared to grow worse instead of better. He finally said my eczema was chroaic, and that I should never be free from it."

" You look well and strong now ; ", interjected the newspaper man. " so tell me what effected your cure." "I am glad to have tke chance of telling you. A young girl who was working in my department of the mill, three or four years ago got so weak that she could not stand, and was only fit to lie down and faint away. She went off work for a fortnight's rest, but got no better. After a while, however, she returned to work quite strong and cheerful, and I was curious enough to ask haw she had managed to overcome her complaint so thoroughly. She replied " I have been cured by two boxes of D. Williams' pink pills for pale people,' and thinking to meself that if the pills had done her g-,01 they should do the same for me. I purchased a box, and after taking the cotta I noticed a slight improvement. I tier punhrsed a second box, and before it was exhaiietal euery sign of the eczema had disappeared from the skin, and the itch- ing sores and other painful eympl-oins had vardshed. I took part of another box, and was as well as ever I was in my lire. This was about a ysear ago, aad I have had no return of the trouble. am now as sound as a bell,and I hope all who are afflicted after the game manner will profit by my experience." It is not nPcessarily in the form of a skin erup!ien that poverty or impurity of the bluni i 3 manifested. Our blood is the cleanser and fao.? carrier of the body, and. anything wrong with it may make itself manifest in a variety of ways—as by aceenia (where thin, watery blood causes pale lips. weakness, languor, headaches, and breathlessnesa); palpitstion of the heart, indigestion (from inability of the bload to absorb nourishment from food taken) : wasting away, a cough and eventually censamntion : or nervousness, St. Vitus' dance, fits, rheumatism. and unhealthy sensitiveness to cold, and even paralyAs. Dr. Williams' pink pills act directly on the blood. Their effect is epeedily seen: thin people put on flesh, rheumatism and coughs diaanpear : there is new life in all the body. But substitut.,s will not give new blood, nor do any other good : the genuine pills are those, and those only, which bear the full name, Dr. Williams' pink pills for pale people. If substitutes are pushed it is best to send direet to Dr. Williams' Medicine Company, Holborn Viaduct, London, enclosing the price —t vo and ninveace for one box ; thirteen and nine for six boxes.

div.head: RSA. MOVEMENT. Wycliffe P.S.A. Society's Tea Meeting.
div.p: THE RSA. MOVEMENT. Wycliffe P.S.A. Society's Tea Meeting.

The most popular social event in connection 1 with Wycliffe P.S.A. S3ciety is the annual tea meet- I ing, and this year's gathering was again a success- ful one. Tea was served in the large schoolroom on Monday evening when about 400 sat down. The tables were presided over by a number of ladies. Excellent arrangements had been made by a small sub-committee composed of Messrs. Fowley, Haw- thorn, Raley, Farrar, and T. Wallington (bon secre- tary.) The:following ladies presided at the tables:— Mesdames J Atkinson,R Atkinson B Farrar,J Birch Colley G F Wommersley,and Bristow,and the Mipses Knowles, Travis, Porritt, Pickavance, Mills, Hill, Dick, Walsh, F Taylor, E Mills, and M Wommers- ley. After tea the party adjourned to the church where a brief organ recital was given by Mr. W H Payton, Mus. Bac. The subsequent proceedings held in the schoolroom were presided over by the Mayor (Alderman Roberts) and be was supported on the platform by the Rev. John Tongs (president of the Society),Councillor Worthington J.P,(Wigan) Mr J Whalley (Manchester), Messrs. S B Stringer, J Bailey, T Hawthorn, T Wallington, B Farrar,lialey, T Atkinson, Woods, Fowley, and others. The Rev. J. YONGE said he wished to be permitted to express in some small way the gratification they all felt in the fact that the Mayor of Warrington was the Chair- man of that meeting. (Applause.) It was not the first time that a Mayer had been mixed to take a position of that kind at a P.S.A. meeting. On a previous occasion the Mayor who was then in office when asked to per- form that office stated that while he appreciated the kindness of the invitation it was not in his line. He was very glad that their present Mayor found it to be in his line to be in their midst that night. (Hear, hear.) In fact, knowing all about teem, they would have been very much disappointed if he had not found it in his line. (He e r, hear.) They were delighted be was there, and they heartily welcomed him. (Applause.) The CHAIRMAN, who was cordially received, said he was very much obliged to them for the hearty and kindly welcome they had extended to him and he must say that while he was no stranger inside those walls it was always a pleasure to him to come when he possibly could to further anything which had to uo with the church to which he belonged. Of course the P.S.A. , institution was an undenominational one. He did not I know it was any the better or worse for that. They Welcomed into their community members of all 1 sections of the Chr:stian 'Church and even those who did not belong to any section of the Church. He found it somewhat difficult to speak on the subject of the P.S.A. movement to any extent, because his knowledge was somewhat limited and his opportunities of being connected with it were alio limi- ted. Re had had to refuse to preside at the meetings because of late years he had been a busy man, and if it were possible he was a still busier man now. (Hear, hear.) He appreciated tne invitation, but he found it , necessary to occupy Sunday in that Way which was most I congenial and most profitable to himself. The work of ' the last three weeks had really been so hard that he became afraid the town would have to appoint someone else if it kept up at the same rate. (Laughter.) But teetotalers required a lot of killing—((aughter)—and either he was getting used to it or the work was begin- ning to get less, it was not telling the same upon his health, and he had not had to resort to auxiliary help in the way some thought necessary when there was a great deal to do. They had been weeding off during the last few weeks, a large number of men who had responded to the call to du:y in a way that did them ,infinite credit and reflected the greatest possible credit on the whole country. We were sending them out to fight our battles, and that night they were going to seed out two ambulance men to help to succour the wounded and nurse the sick. (Applause.) It would be his privilege as well as his great pleasure when he left that meeting to say a few words of good cheer on their behalf and his own. (Applause) Theme two men were going out with the two-fold object in view of fighting our battles and nursing the sick and wounded. These two ideas ought to find a large plaeo kr the work of the P.S.A. Society. They wanted to train men to fight our battles—our moral battles and public battles ; to fight battles where they knew a little bit of pluck, a little bit of courage. and a litt'e bit of honest truth telling might be of service to the whole community. (Per, hear.) I One of the main objects and successful results woich had , followed the P.S.A. bad been the fact that the members ' were getting much more interested in their daily responsi- bilities—the responsibilities which rested upon every

man every day in the week both at his work and in his Leisure. Then in connection with the P.S.A. they had a band of workers specially appointed to help the sick. The object was a noble One and ought to commend itself ' to everybody.(Applause.) He appreciated fully the kir '- nese ehevoa to him in the heartiness of their welcome "that tught-and he also appreciated the kindness which had been shown by the whole town to him. (Hear, hear.) That was the first opportunity he bad had of publicly expressing his intense gratitude to his fellow tewnsasen who had honoured him so conspicuously by their pre' - ence and association with him at public functions on the Last few occasions, lie would like to speak a word of encouragement to the young men present. They would have many a disappointment,many a battle to fight and they would lose many a one, but if they persevered success would ultimately be theirs. Be believed be was himself an exemplification of that fact. (Hear, hear.) He had been a fighting man for 27 years and he hoped he should be a fighting man for 27 years to come, possibly with greater tact and greater wisdom and perhaps with less ebullition of temper. He appre- ciated his own failings quite as much as those on the other aide. (Laughter.) But with better knowledge he hoped it might be his let to keep them in the back- ground and do all he possibly could to promote the material, social aud moral welfare of the people of the town and those whom be loved most sincerely. (Ap- plause.) Councillor WORTHINGTON of Wigan. remarked that it was a pleasure to him to attend the P.S.A. meeting and to meet the Mayor as chairman ef it. He happened to have lived in Warrington at one time and he then be- came acqueinted with its present Mayor. He was sure Alderman lisborts would reflect very great credit on the chair, and he should not be at all surprised if those who had disagreed with the Mayor would once again agree at the end of his term of office to re-eleot him to the poiition again. (Hear, bear.) He (Mr. Worthington) would not have come to speak at that meeting unless he felt that the Wycliffe P.S.A.was exercising a very strong religious influence upon the town. The speaker pro- ceeded to dwell on the importance of building up a character and pursuing a career worthy of them. ' Mr. WHALLEY of Manchestersin referring to the Chair- man's remarks as to being a teetotaler, said he had been a teetotaler for f4ver 40 years and had been doing his best to kill the liquor traffic. He had met with a great deal of opposition and some of it was of a peculiar char- acter. He was glad to hear that the Mayor was so decided an this important point and that at the public receptions he was true to his principles. (Hear, bear), If the Mayor continued to the end of his year of office as he had begun, when he handrd his seals of Office over to his successor he would do so with the conciousness of having done his duty and with the approval of every intolligent and rightminded inhabitant of the Borough. (Applause.) The speaker proceeded to refer to the bene- fits to be derived from the P.S.A. Society, and in a humorous manner referred to the influence which *omen cauld exer, in getting men to attend the meetings. He concluded his remarks by some suggestions on how to make life happy. An excellent musical proerararne was provided. Miss Walsh successfully sang " When the been is young," and " The Carnival." Mr. Arthur Griffith's pure toned tenor voice was heard to great advantage in the solo "Mary of Argyle" and in response to a well deserved encore he complied with " The King's Own." He also sang in company with George Clay, jun., in the duet " Lova and War." Mr. George Clay was indisposed, hut nevertheless he sang well.and was loudly applauded for his siagineof "Wilt o' the Wisp." Mr W H Peyton Mos. Bar.. played the pianoforte accomeanimeet. Mr El M Ashton gave in his notedly clever manner a humorous reading. A pleasant evening was broueht to a close by the acknowledgment of the services of the Mayor, the speakels and others in connection with the gatherine on the proposition of Me Stringer, seconded by Mr Haley.

div.head: Sad Fatality to a Servant Girl at
div.p: The Sad Fatality to a Servant Girl at
Grappenhall.

Sir,—The information as given by you on the above to the effect that the poor girl's neck aas tick( n need I think be received by yourself, and the public with the greatest caution. My information and from what should be a reliable source was to the effect that the neck was not broken,and those who laid out the corpse and assisted in doing so could see nothing to indicate that such was the case. As to the Police evidence. He simply taw the lifeless form, and knew nothing more about the cause of death than did the Jury, and his evidence could shrew no extra light upon the matter. The only one who could properly account for the sad termination to so young a lire was the deccased person herself.—l am sir, yours obediently,

div.head: STEPHEN H. JENKINS.
div.p: STEPHEN H. JENKINS.

The more Mr. Jenkins writes about this sad affair and the more he strengthens our contention that the coroner's enquiry was of a perfunctory character. He also has bad Information from "a raliatrle source "with regard to the assertion that the giri's neck was broken. Why was none of this " reliable information" on so important a point given at the inquest ? The body of Miss Jeffs was sees by both a constable and a medical man, and yet neither was called to testify to what was, in their opinion, the cause of death. Again we ask why? though we do not expect that our correspondent can answer the ques- tiou.—laß. " Ex."

Sir—Will you grant me space in your next issue for a few words on the above subject. I think it looks very bad for the police and the coroner that so mysterious a death should be so lightly dealt with. I see Mr. Stephen Jenkins thinks he has, with the others, done his duty as a juryman as far as it lay in their power in bringing in the verdict "Found drowned." (You may _well ask how they came to this conclusion without medical testimony en the cause of death). Are the jury not allowe .1 to pass their own verdict or does the Cheshire coroner do it for them ? As one who has sat on a jury I have always found it our duty to consider the evidenc:, and pass our owra verdict. I am really surprised at a jury of elderly men being led away in this manner,and Las brother of the thceased,girl,do cos- sider it my duty to publicly make known the fact that I am not at all satisfied with the verdict or the way he which the evidence was got up. I have seen many cases of far less importance than this looked into in every possible way, and the more one thinks of it, the more the mystery deepens. The doctor who examined her, the gardener who found her, and the police were not called to give evidence. Who is to blame for this: the police or the Coroner ? If you can tell us who is responsible for this state of affairs I, with others, would be extremely obliged to you.—l am yours truly, L. JEFFS.
23. Bedford-road, Birkdale, Southport. November 30, 1899.

The police are the authority resronsible for getting'to- gether the evidence to be tendered at an inquest but the coroner may require any additional witness to be called whom he msy wish to bear. We have receivc I a long letter which we cannot find room for, on this rame subject, from a correspondent signing himself " One Deeply Interested," and who also expresses dissatisfaction at the way the inquest was con- ducted. He suggests exhumation and further inquiry, but we do not think there is anything in the case to call for such extreme measures.—ED. " Ex."

div.head: Town Clock Degenerate.
div.p: The Town Clock Degenerate.

Sir,—May I ba allowed to ask through the medium of your paper w fly the Town Clock has been for some months past several minutcs wrong. Fortunately this error has been on the side likely to cause the least annoyance, inasmuch as it is in advance of the time re- corded by the Post Office and Railway Telegraph Office. Yet in view of letters one remembers to have seen eman- ating from the late Mr. F. Reynolds setting forth the virtues arid performances of the cicck it is somewhat disappointing to Eee it so degenerate. Were the fault in the opposite direction, and those people who arrive to meet the Liverpool and Manchester trains just in the nick of time, to find that they were two or three minutes late instead of that amount early, it is highly probable some enquiry would have been made earlier than this.—Yours truly,

div.head: TIMEKEEPER.
div.p: TIMEKEEPER.
The Reservists' Families.

Sir,—The parting of these men from their wives and families is very distressing, more so than those who have not to undergo it can realise. There is a grand and praiseworthy effort being made by the inhabitants in every town, to raise money to relieve the families of those men who have been taken away to fight for their country, and it is intended, and wished for, that this relief should prevent them from becoming paupers, or applying to the Board of Guardians for out-relief. This all sounds very Dice, and it would be well if it could be so, but will it do this? No ;I, who have had large ex- perieece in granting out-relief say at once that it will not. Now we will take a woman left with four children It is I suppose intended to give her 5s per week, and is nee week foreach child,9s in all. Putting it at the lowest, 3s 6d will have to be paid for rent, say nothing about coal, clothing, &e., and what has she left to shape on? Of course her husband's small pay will do a little if she can get it. It is simply cruel to contemplate the misery that will ensue, and there will be worse cases than this. Repeatedly we have cases coming before us as Guardians, of widows and children being left similar to the one I have meationed,and we think the cases sufficiently hard to warrant us in giving them perhaps from 3s to 43 per week. These widows with what they can probably earn themselves may be in receipt of about 8s per week besides. The families of those taken away will piece them on a level with these. What I want to point out sir, is this, that the intentions of the subscribers to the fund to keep the families of these men from becoming nargeable to the parish will not be accomplished, and theretore I main- tain that the Guardians, however they may wish tot avoid it, will have to give relief to these people ; there- fore it comes to what I should like to say that if these men are to be forced away to fight for their country, the Government should be responsible for their families' maintenance,but failing this,and the Board of Guardians are applied to, I trust they will be as liberal as they can, and that the ratepayers will not grudge the money spent, and above all that the chargeability will not de- prive then' of their futere political rights.—Yours trulf, S. D. November 30th, 1899.

div.head: ASTHMA CAN BE CURED.

div.head: EXAMINER FRIDAY, DECEMBER 8. 1899
div.p: THE EXAMINER FRIDAY, DECEMBER 8. 1899
NEWTON URBAN DISTRICT COUNCIL. -

A meeting of this Council was held in the Town Hall, Earlestown, OD Monday evening. Mr. C. B. F. Borron, J.P., C.C., preiidei, and there were also present : Dr. Patten-:, Al.,:,srs. J. W. Emmett, J.P., W Gilmour, E. Stone, J.P., J. Simpson, William Thompson, W. Beatty, J. H. Forster, E. T. Evan, 'f. Ormand, w. Collingwood, N. liddelly, with W. W. Shirley (clerk), 4 B )wes (sur- veyor), aid D. H. Lloyd (gas engineer.)

div.head: LATE MR. BRIERLEY.
div.p: THE LATE MR. BRIERLEY.

• At an extraordinary meeting of the Urban District Council, held at the Town Hall Earlestown, on Monday November 20, it was reeolved " That this G.oncii hav- ing heard with deep regret of the death of Richard Brierley, Esq., of Earlestown. for 30 years Cierk and Surveyor to the Newten-in-3,lakerfield Improvement Commissioners and Urban District Council, desires to express its appreciation and recognition of the valuable services rendered by Mr. Brierley, and to place upon re- cord its deep regret at the great loss the Council have sustained by his death, and that a copy of this resolu- tion be forwarded to Mrs. Brierley, as a respectful ex- pression to her and her sorrowing fsmily of the sympa- thy and condolence of every member of this Council in their bereav meet."

The Chairrn•in said the following letter had been re- ceived from Mrs. Brierley : "I beg to thank you most heartily on behalf of myself and family for the kisd ex- pression of sympathy and condolence conveyed in the resolution forwarded by Mr. Shirley on th.: 21st inet. I also take this opportunity of thanking you for the kind- ness and leniency shown to ray late husband during the last few months of his term of office,—Yours etc., ELLEN ERIERLEY."
GAS AND WATER COMMITTEE. STOKERS AND THEIR WAGES.

At a meeting of this committee it was ordered that tenders be invited for the purchase 3f coke during the year 1900, in not less than 50 ton lots, to be loaded and carted away by the parchaser. The Gasworks Extensions Committee to accept the contracts. It was resolved that the matter be left in the engineer's hands with the power to make such terms by way of compensation as may appear to him just and equitable. —A letter dated 15th November, was read from the stokers at the Gasworks, requestine a reply at once to their application for an increase of wages, and stating that otherwise they would be cumpelled to cease work at the expiration of one week from this date; whereupon it was resolved that the Clerk reply, stating that the application is being carefully considered by the commit- tee, and a reply would be forwarded as soon as possible, and that any alterations in the scale of pay now obtain- ing would date from Saturday, the 25th iustant, and that the committee regret that they should have seen fit to send such a letter to them, and to request its with- drawal immediately. It was also resolved that it be an instru^tien t 3 the Gasworks Extensions Committee to take steps to provide workmen to take the places at shore netice of any of the Council's workmen who may threaten to come out on strike as in the case of the stokers. The report of the Gasworks Extens'ons Commit- tee was read as follows,viz :—" (a) Your sub-committee have appointed Mr. J. E. Gee, of Earlestown, as chief meter inspector, at a wage of 28s. per week with uni- form, Messrs. E. A. Whitehead, Newton-le-Willows, and E. P. Cleworth, of Leigh, as assistant meter inspectors, at a wage of 235. per week each, also with uniform. (b) The sub-committee recommend the acceptance of the tender of Mr. E. Bunting, of the sum of £B4. for con- verting the old purifying house into a photometer room. (c) They also recommend the appointment of a water meter inspector to examine all water pipes,and to report as to defective fittings." It was resolved that the fore- going report be approved and adopted. A letter dated the 13th November, was read from Messrs. Fletcher, Russell and Co., of Warrington, applying for permission to hold a gas cooking exhibition in this town, subject to cartain conditions. Alter consideration it was resolved that the committee cannot see their way to accede to ' the application on the lines suggested. A letter, datedl the 17th November, was read from the Engine Boiler, &c., Insurance Co., stating that so far as examination could be made the boilers at the gasworks were in good condition.
Mr. Emmett asked whether the letter which was sent by the stoker 3 had !poen withdrawn.

The Chairman : Yes ; a letter was received,signed by the men, unconditionally withdrawing the notices sent. Mr. Gilmour : That is all right. (Hear, hsar.) The minutes were then passed. HIGHWAYS AND SANITARY COMMITTEE. RESIGNATION OF MR. GREGORY.

At a meeting of the above mentioned committee it was resolved that the following building plans be approved and passed viz : —Tower, S.: Peter's Church ; proposed streets; Lord Newton ; Eli Bunting: 13 houses. Nev lle.street, John Harrison : 3 houses, Wargrave-read Two letters dated the 10th and 13th of November, 1899, were submitted from Mr. J. W. Knowles, solicitor, of Widnes, and owner of certain premises situate in Brad- legh-road, Wargrave ; the Clerk stated that Mr. Knowles was taking exception to the final apportionment served upon him in respect of his proportion of the cost of the makir g of Bradlegh-road ;that be (the Clerk) had already written him on the matter, and that Mr. Knowles bad lodged with him a formal objec- tion to the apportionment, whereupon it was resolved, that the matter be placed in Messrs. Peace and Ellis's hands. A letter dated the 28th October was read from the Deputy Clerk of the Lancashire County Council stating that he had no doubt but that some arrangement could be made whereby the payment of the grant for the flagging of Church-street could be deferred until the corcpletion of the tower of S. Peter's Church. A letter dated the 9th November was read from the L. and N.-W. Railway Company,having reference to the improvement of Railway-street, agreeing to the pro- posals of the Council, but that the Railway Company would not accept any responsibility with regard to the closing of the wicket gate. It was ordered that the Clerk endeavour to prevail upon the Railway Company to accept the responsibility of the closing of the gate referred to. It was also resolved that the Council be recommended to sewer, level, pave, flag, channel, and otherwise make good so much of Haydock-street as lies between Stanley-street and Heather Brae, Earlestown, ' and that upon completion of the said work the owners of premises fronting, joining, or abutting upon the said street be charged with the cost thereof. Letters dated ' the 16th and 18th November, were read from Messrs. Peace and Ellis, solicitors, with reference to the appeals —refusal to pay tolls—in the matters of the Council v. Brown, and v. Lyon, from which it appeared that Mr. Riley,policitor to the two defendants, proposed that if the Council would withdraw the appeals and ask for no costs hie clients were prepared to undertake to nay the Wits for the future, and not to;initiate or concur in any movements against the tolls. Messrs. Peace and Ellis further stated that they considered Mr. Ril y's proposal too one-sided for acceptance, and were of opinion that the Council ought not to withdraw the appeale ; where- upon it was resolved that Mr. Riley's proptehl he not entertained. It was also resolved that the question of the appointment of a sanitary inspector, as well as the reorganization of the sanitary department, be referred to a committee consisting of Councillors Collingwood, Borron (J.P.), Stone (J.P.), SMepson, Patterson,Forster, and Ormand. It was ordered that the Clerk inform the Local Government Board of the death of Mr. Brierley, late Sanitary Inspector, and apply for their sanction to pay to his representatives his salary up to the 31st December, 1899. At a meeting of the Highways and Sanitary Com- mittee held on Monday afternoon, a letter dated the 29th of November was read from Mr. John Gregory re- signing his position as toll collector, marker inspector and assistant sanitary inspector to take effect on the 31st December,whereupon it was resolved that the committee accept with regret Mr. Gregory's resignation. A letter bearing the same date, was read from Mr: A. Bowes, surveyor, asking that some improvement might be made in his position. It was resolved that Mr. Bowes' letter be referred to the Office sub-committee for their con- sideration and report. It was ferther resolved that it be a recommerdation to the Highways and Sanitary Committee that an inspector of nuisances be appointed at a commencing salary of £lOO per annum rising to £l2O per annum ; camlidates to be members of the Sani- tary Institute or prepared to qualify within twelve months of his appointment ; the collection of tolls for ' both market and street hawking to be done by the in- spector of nuisances. The Sub-Committee also suggested that a night foreman of the night soil department should be appointed when the new inspector of nuisances takes up office. The minutes were passed on the proposition of Mr. Collingwood. The Chairman said they would observe that an old servant had considered it his duty to retire. GENERAL PURPOSES COMMITTEE. POST OFFICE ACCOMMODATION.

At a meeting of the General Purposes Committee it was resolved that the Tramways Committee be em- powered, if in their opinion it appears to be necessary to engage Messrs. Peace and Ellis, of Wigan, solicitors, to act on behalf of the Council with regard to the scheme of the South Lancashire Tramways Company: A letter datid the 16th November was read from the Secretary to the General Post Office, London, stating, in reply to the Clerk's letter, that it had not yet been found practi- cable to arrange for improved accommodation at the Earlestown Post Office, but hoped that a satlement wou'd shoitly be Come to. It was ordered that the Clerk again communicate with the General Post Office and state that their letter was considered very unsatisfac- tory, and askon to be furnished with more definite in- formation,

Mr. Emmett 3.,tred whether any reply had ben re- ceived from the Post Office. The Chairman read the folflwing Itter : " General Post Office. With reference 4o your further letter of the 22ad int. I am directed to inform you that the proposals for improvine the accommodation at tho Earlestown Post Office are now before the Lords Corn miAsioners and tile Treasury have been requested to con vey their decision in the matter as soon as possible." Tho minutes were then passed.

div.head: WAR.
div.p: THE WAR.

LATEST TELEGRAMS. Another Attack on Ladysmith Furious Engagement. Boers Driven Back. Dukater, DEC. 5. News brought in by runners to Frera camp, states that the enemy made what is thought to have been their last great effort to capture Ladyealiii early on Monday morning. The bombardment was furious for some hours but did little or no damage. We subsequently silenod their guns, and a sortie was made. Hard fighting is reported ta have followed, the Boers retreating after very heavy losses estimated at several hundreds. It is now prebable that the Boers have decided to abandon the siege. Large commandoes has been observed moving in the direction cf tbe Free State border. Graver Situation. The "Time*" special correspondent telegraphs via Pietermaritzburg, Ladysmith, December 2 : The situation is becoming graver. The enemy are showing more system in their artillery fire. They con- centrate it upon given points, with the result that con- siderable damage ia done to the town and to property. Official news from Ladysmith states that on November 30th there were 207 Fick in the beseiged -- town and 225 wounded.
Lord Methuen in Communi- cation with Kimberley.
CAPMOWN, WEDNESDAY. Methuen wires to-day he has resumf d command. Is in nightly communication with Kimberley. Health of troops excellent.

div.head: Modder River Polluted by Dead Boers.
div.p: Modder River Polluted by Dead Boers.

CAPETO • ' One despatch from Modder River states that the river has been seriously pollutel by the number of dead bodies of Boers which the enemy threw into it during the fighting last Tuesday. It is thought the majority of the Indies are tho3e of the enemy bayoneted by the North- umberlands in their charge.

div.head: CHARITY CONCERT AT THE PUBLIC HALL, RUNCORN.
div.p: CHARITY CONCERT AT THE PUBLIC HALL, RUNCORN.

The grand concert, given at the Public Hall,Runcorn. on Wednesday evening, by the St. Paul's Church choir, in aid of Robert Hemp, of 32, Bridgewater-street, who through an accident had lost his eyesight and was con- sequently depi:ved of his ordinary means of livelihood, proved a huge success, and a very handsome sum was realised for the object. The chair was occupied by Mr. F. J. Norman. In a short address he referred to the grand wave of benevolence that was passing over the country in connection with the patriotic and other funds in aid of the soldiers in the Transvaal, and remarked that in Runcorn at least there were evidences th,t they had opt forgotten their ordinary duty, and at any rate they were carrying out the .naxim that "many could help one, if one could not help many "and meant to keep poor Bob out of the four wails of Dutton Work- house. (Applause.) The programme opened with "Rule Britannia "by the St. Paul's Choir. Mr. James Weedall St. Helens, folio wed with a happy rendition of" In Happy Moments (" Maritana"). In the second part he gave "Soldiers of the Queen and was recalled. The large auc.;ence joined in the chorus with enthusiasm. Miss But y (St. Helens) was very successful in "The Flight of Ages " and "When the heart is young; for encore she sang " Kilarney " and with such effect as to receive warm acknowledgement. As a cornet soloist Mr. T. Knight excelled in both his contributions " All Through the Night" and " Annie Laurie." Tne Run- corn Male Voice Choir (under the conductorship of Mr C Leathwood) contributed " Soldiers Chorus" (Faust), "Comrades in Arms ' ; and "The long day closes "as an encore, which was proof of due appreciation. " I seek thee in every flower" and " 0 that summer smiled for aye !" were two tasteful tenor songs given by Mr A Jones (St. Helens). For the latter he received a unanimous recall and ob:iged witn a Welsh version of the same song. Mr Craddock submitted a selected flute solo. Miss Siinkin tor the "Soldier's Dream' was deservedly applauded- But the duet " 0 that we two were maying,” by Miss Simkin and Mr J Weedail, proved a combination of baritone and contralto that did At take. fne sc. Patil'a choir (conclu:ttor Mr T Taylor Burrows), were responsible for " Tis Day Wedding Morning" (F H Cowen's, "Rose bitaiden"), and "Worthy is the Lamb" (Handel), both of which were finished and masterly performances. Two comic items were contributed by Mr J Beckett. The accompanist was Mr George Bowyer, organist ot St Paul's Church.— Mr W Byfleltl, 3.3, Thomas-street, Runcorn the treasurer, of the movement, publicly thanked all who had contributed to the success of of the entertainment, on behalf of Mr. Robert Elarrop, who was present esconced in arm chair on the platform. —Mr. Nsrm In having read :1 sympathic latter from Sir John Brunner Bart. M.P., in which he enclosed £3 3s, towards the cause; remarked such letters from Sir John Brunner did not come as a surprise to them as his name was becoming, in Runcorn,synonomous with unbounded generosity. (Applause.)—At the Chairman's request the aunience rose and sing "God Save the Queen " three times, as a protest against the abuses impudent foreigners had hurled at our gracious Queen.

div.head: BIRD -8 HUW.
div.p: BIRD -8 HUW.
Opening by the Mayor.

The members of the Warrington, Penketh and Distric Cage Bird and Pigeon Fancier's Asseciation held their fourth annual show of canaries, males, British and foreign birds and pigeons in the Parr Hall on Saturday afternoon. Excellent arrangements had been made by a committee caneisting ef the following gentlemen : President, Mr T blather, ; Vice-eresidents, Messrs. W Rogers, J W Johnson, H Clare, F L)ckyer, W Leigh. Committee, Messrs. E Page, J Hampson, F Burrows, J Wilson, R Barker. Treasurer, Mr. S Both. Hon, Sec., Mr E R Godwin ; Assistant secretary, Mr. F Boyle. There was a record number of entries viz , 131 in the pigeon classes and 169 in the cage bird classes. Some fine birds were exhibited, the gold medal for the best British bird being wen by Mr. J Hampson. The judges were Messrs. C Hnulton of St. Helens and J Heald, jun., of Choriey and their awards gave generai satisfaction. The proceeds ev,re in aid ot the Mayer's Transvaal Cam- paign Relief Fund. In the evening the Bor. Jugh Bind who pave their services played selections. Several of the exhibits were sold ,and the amounts realized devoted Co the fund. The show was opened at 2.30 by his Wor- ship the Mayor (Alderman H Roberts, J.P.) The PRESIDENT (Mr. T. Mather), in asking the Mayor to open the show said the society felt deeply indebted to his Worship for his kindness in coming amongst them.

The MAYOR, in opening the show, said that he was very pleased to be present as he was a bird fernier himself. He was never an exhibitor but a breeder. Birds had always a great attraction for him. When they studied the habits of the wild bird, its form and shape, the colour of its feathers and the construction and position of its nest they found that all departments oi bird life were vary Pr.eresting. A. student of natural history could not have a more interesting science than the study of birds. He thought they were performing A very useful function in forming a society for the en- couragement of the breeding of cage bilds and in go!.- ting more and more people engaged in everything that pertained t 3 the showing and breeding of them. H. hoped that the scciety would persevere in this very laudable object and get more memb3rs every year. The show that day was a highly creditable one. In conclusion he advised those who had not ob- tained prizes to persevere and probably the time would soon come when they would be priz 3 winners. Like everything else the breeding and showing of birds was a science which required a great deal of 3i:tidying and a man must not expect to win pnizs at once. If he was patient and persevered ,success would crown his efbrte. It had given him (Alderman Roberts) very great pleariure to be present and he wished the society every possible success. He had now great pleasure in declaring the show open. (Applause.) On the motion of Mr S. FAY, seconded by Mr. E. R. Gonwne, a vote of thanks was accorded with acclaim- motion to the Mayor for opening the show. The MAYOR in responcling,said he was very grateful to the Society for deoiding to give the pro?-eeds to ,he fund for the relief of the wives and families of the reservists.
