div.head: FOR THE FRONT.
div.p: FOR THE FRONT.
Departure of Warrington Ambulance
Men.

It is a matter of congratulation that two members of the Warrington Corps of the St. John Ambnilance Brigade have been selected, alter examination, for service in South Africa as first-class hospital orderlies. The corps is in number four district which includes Lancashire. Cheshire, Cumberland, Westmoreland, and Ireland, and there are between sixty and seventy corps altogether in the district. Out of these only sixteen men have been seleeted so that it is highly creditable that Warrington should supply two out of so small a number. The men are Privates IL Holloway and J. E. Newns,andnre both employed on the Cheshire Lines Railway. Tee former is a booking-clerk and Nemo is in the engineering department. Holloway is also a member of the Volunteer Corps. Both of the men have gained distinction in ambulance examinations anl competitions. They left Warrington for Loedon late on Monde} night, and their comrades deter- mined that they should have a hearty "send off." At seven o'clock the members of the corps assembled at the Gymnasium and marched in procession, headed by the Borough Band by way of Bridge- street, Horsemarket-street, Winwick-street,Tanners- lane, Bewsey-street, Horsemarket-street, Sankey- street, and Parker-street. to the Patten Arms Ho'el. Unfortunately the weather was very unfavourable, and consequently not many spectators assembled on the route. A large number congregated owside the Hotel, and as Nawns and Holloway entered, a hearty cheer was raised. The company adjourned to the large room and a "hot pot "was served. After the tables had been cleared, the remainder of the evening was spent in a convivial manner. Mr. P. Rylands presided, and amongst those present were :—Drs. Adams and Smith, Lieutenant G. R. Crosfield, Mr. A. 11. Crosfield, Captain Waring, Superintendent Buckley, and Mr. T J. Hulse. Later in the evening the Mayor (Alderman Roberts), and the ex-Mayor (Alderman Wright) put in an appear- ance. The toasts "The Queen" and " The Prince of Wales " were musically honoured, after which several songs and other items were contributed. Private Newns provoked much laughter with the humorous song " Hooligan's Mu'" and was ont hu- siastically encored, singing in response "More work for the undertaker." Mr. J. Taylor sang " Soldiers of the Queen." the company joining heartily in the chorus. Mr. A. H. Crosfield accompanied the hearty singing of" Hearts of Oak." A recitation was given by Mr. Clegg with good effect, and the concertina solos by Mr. Whittaker were well received. During the evening _ _ _

Lieutenani G. R. CROSFIILD announced that the fol- lowing had pass•d the nursing examination :—Superin- tendent J G Buckley ; let officer H Williams; 2nd officer C Mannsuer; Privates. H Holloway, J ENewne, Bagley, J Dimelow, and I Malkin. Dr. ADAMS said there were tea volunteers and the names read out were those of the nen who had after a very short course of instruction passed an examination by Dr. Darwin who was not the easiest of examiner,. After a song had been rendered by Mr. W. D. Fell,

Dr. ADAMS said there was just ens toast that they ought not to forget. He had not been asked to propose it, but as Privates Holloway and Newne were "his own boys "he was going to do so. The toast was that of the two volunteers for the South African field forces under the auspices of the Red Cross Slciety, being mem-ers of the St. John Ambulance Brigade, and holding both first aid and nursing certificates—Privates Holloway and Noway. They all knew them very well. On the roll call of the brigade their names figured as conspicuously in regard to atteadance as those at any rate, of most of the other members. Dr Adams went on to speak of the irregular attendance at parades of some of the memb' rs, and in conclusion said that Privates Holloway and Newns were two of the most efficient men in the corps. He bad writ- ten:4l letter te Dr Trimble, the Deputy Commissioner telling him that they were two good men. He under- stood they would go with the Duke of Portland's detach- ment, the Duk3 of Portland having giving £lO,OOO to the cause. He should not be surprised if the remaining six who had passed the examination were not called up- on. tie asked them to rise and give a'good send off and a hearty cheer for the two voluntters who were being sent out.
The toast was enthusiastically drunk, cheers were given, and the company sang " For they are jolly good fellows."

Private HOLLOWAY in responding said he was very pleased with the "send of!" they hed given he and Private Newns that night, and be should always do his best to get a good report of their work sent. He was very glad of the opportunity of serving his country as an Englishman and he should try and do it thoroughly. When he Came back to the corps he should come among them as a fellow member. (Hear, hear.) He wee very thankful and begged to express his thanks to Dr. Adams for "getting them through" so rapidly. (Ap- plause.) Instead of making a speech Private Newns gave a recitation "Christmas day in the Workh,use." Dr. ADAMS read letters Private Holloway had re- ceived from Major Boerne, adjutant of the let V B.S. Lancashire Reeiment, and Colonel Rideway, the officer of the company with which Holloway was connected. The former wished him success in his duty and " God speed "in his journ .y. Colenel Ridgway said it wa.. very gratifying to all the regiment that one of their members was going to South Africa and especially to himself, and to " F "Company, that they seould be the first cOmoany to send a man away. He hops 3 that when Private Holloway got out to Africa he would do his best for the poor fellows who needed his care. He hoped he would have a pleasant voyage and a safe return home. (Applause.) Captain WARING said that as their chief superintec- dent he felt very proud that two of their men were going out for service in Bauch Africa. He felt certain that, they would attend to the lick and wounded in a most intelligent and careful manner and give satisfaction to the patients and the medical officers. It was very pleasing to those who had taken an interest in ambul- ance work that these men had been chosen frem the good old town of Warrington—(applause)—ani that they could supply more if required whilst towns like Liver- pool and Manchester could not send a tingle man. The corps was formed in February 1897, and they had now over a hundred members, and fifty officers and men in uniform, and eec,ind to none in the county. ([leer, hear) This was partly due to the enthusiasm of the men. They had had a helping hand from many kind friends amnegst whom be might mention the Crosfield family.—(Applause.)—Mr. J. Chariton Parr who was away from horns and sent a telegram wi hing the men "Gid speed "and a safe return and who had also sent them each a present ; Mr. and Miss Naylor who for- warded a donation and were sorry that they could not attend ; Mr. T. J. Down and his band; Mr. W. B. Roberts,Mr J. Malin Edlesten and the late Mr. T. Morris. Mrs. and Miss Crosfield sent caps for the men. If the eotice had not been so short they would have had tam o' shanters too, Mr. Harry Toft sent R suitable gift. In conclusion he asked the men ti obey orders and do their duty diligently and well, to fear G•cl and hate the devil,and they w auld return with a bright experience of what other countries were like, and he hoped well and hearty, (Applause.) The Chairman then handed a cake of tobacco to each et the men the gift of Mr. Harry Toff. The CRAIRMAN proposed the toast of " The St. John Ambulance Brigade." He said that war was undoate- tedly a terrible thing, but it was war that had made the British Empire what it was, and it was war which had made the British man what he was—the finest man in the world. So long as the British empire was what it was, so long there would be war. So long as the Brit;sh soldier was what he was, so long there would b 3 a British Empire. The operations in Smith Africa were not an uadefensible attack on other people's property, but a resistance against the attack of the Dutchman. If those operations had taught them one thing, it was that the British soldier was as fine a man as ever he was. (Applause) So long as the British Empire had to depend upon such men as these, they had nothing to fear. He thought they would agree that the horrors of war were generally. mitigated by the great efforts made by volen any asseciations and more particularly by the St. John's Ambulance Brigade in tending the wounded in the time of battle One of the greatest horrors of war used to be the small facility for looking after and giving medical comforts to wounded men. Now, men were prepared to risk tl eir lives in aiding the wounded and in pitigstihse their sufferings and the St. Jehn Ambul- ance Brigade was right in the fore front. Nothing could be more splendid or admirable than the way in which it had furnished skilled, trained men to reo forward as volunteers and undertake perhaps the most important we-k that could be done to the brave soldiers who were lighting. He had pleasure in proposing the toast and coupled with it, the name of Captain Waring. The toast was drunk with great enthusiasm and cheers were given for the Mayor, Dr. Adams, Mr. Cros- fiald and ethers.

The M&T m Qaid he was very glad to be present that nigh,. for two or three reasons. Be was glad b-cause th 1 Chairmal wis the son of the late Mr. Peter Rvlands. (Applause.) He was sot going to talk politics, that vs not the occasion for it. but it was ancient hi9tory no, , he thought, that 119 (tho Mayor) workM for his (the (liairrnan's) father in 1868 as a lad r and in 1874 as an o Mal. Ho hoped that the good work begun bv his (the c airman's) grandfather in connection with the civic lifo o the town acd for its best develop- ment, and maintaiked and expanded so nobly by his

ALL COUNTRY PEOPLE should read The Rural World id. weekly, which contains articles on Horses, Cattle, the Dairy, Poultry, Bees, ItObbits, Pigs, Gardening, Natural History. Botany of the Parka and Garden, the Home, Foreign and Colonial Intelligence. Anwers to Correspondents, etc. It is profusely illustrated and is altogether, a most int erest- ing and instructive farming and country paper. A good medium for servants requiring situations. The Manager offers to send a specimen free. The address is 110 and 11 STEWCD, Louden, W.—Advt, 1

father and his brother would find a fitting hereditary successor in him (the chairman). The name of Hylanes was a household word in Warrington and worthily so. H. hop,d none of them would live to see the day when it shou'd ceasa to be associated with all that was best, iii truest aud noble.st in the public He of the town. They hoped las would and expected him (the chairman) to eo something to worthily maintain that which had been so long connected with his family. (Applause.) Ha was glad to be present for another reason. He was glad to find that one of the two young fellows was a son Of an eld school fellow of his. He had got to •.n age when perhaps he could appreciate even better than ever he could before, the friendships and connections that one made at school. He was glad to know that Holloway's father was still alive and he hoped doing well in the good old town. They were close friends years ago and he did not tnink their connection had ceased now although their paths in life had been divided. He was not sure whether Newns's father was not an old school fellow, hut whether he was or not, he admired fully the fact that he and Holloway had been selected for that important duty in South Africa. He thought that not only was the honour a great one to the 'nea,but it reflected rquallv great honour on the medical man who had t •ained them for that service—(applause) —and it refleetei hoeour on the company to which they belonged. Speaking, as he thought he might, as the voice of the whole town, he said that every man and woman in Warrington was proud of the fact that this honour was reflectad on the town. The town had been singled out to send two men out of a comparatively' small number, while much larger towns in the immedi- ate neighbourhood were still outside in the cold. (Ap- plause.) Whatever opinioas there might be as to the neceasities or other wise of war and he was afraid they were feeling and sensibly feeling that there was more than one side to it, before many months they sticuld feel that eiCe a great deal more than they did now. While they felt he seriousness of war they valued the bravery, the determination, the pluck and the eedur- ance which our soldiers had shown in South Africa. (Applause.) They felt as they never felt before, that the old country had now thousands and thousands of men ready to follow the flag wherever it went and respond to the call that Queen or country might make upon them. There might be opinions and differences between them as to the cause of the war, but there could be no two opinions as to the duties and obligations which the St. John Ambulance Brigade had taken upon itself in regard to the operations in South Africa. They had one of the noblest and one of the dearest duties to perform and one of the sweetest actions ever possible for m n to do. He knew that Privates Newns and Hollo- way would do their duty well. They hoped the time would be short that they would have to remain in Africa ana thee would give them such a welcome when they came back—(applause)—which would more than recompense them for auy self sacrifice they might have to give. They would have to give some; they would have to be ready at any hour of the day or night to per- form duties. But he knew they would do it,because the same spirit was animating them that had animated all the men who had responded so nobly in this hour of ' trouble. He was glad to have had that opportunity of speaking to them and he wished them "God speed" and a speedy and safe return. (Applause.) Mr. A. H. Creosergen during the Course of a few re- marks commented on the enthusiastic character of the meeting. He said that the assembly rang as true as all assembles of English people did at this moment. The first time that the ambulance brigade in this town was prominently brought under his n tics, was during the frequent journeys he took on the Cheshire Lines Ra - way. He then had many a conversation with their friend, and his friend he thought he might all him, Mr. Hardy, the late secretary. Speaking of ties war, he said the Mayor had alluded to possible misgivings about the way in which the war Came about. He heartily gr ed wit 'i hi 11 t .at that was not the time for them to c ,naider matiere of that kind. During the last few days he had been reading the reminiscences of a very great American who visited these shores fifty years ago and he spoke ot the reserve force in the British nation. He said that in goad times they might find the Englishman, was a drowsy customer but they did not know the re- serve force and the grit tnat was in him till there was a time of strces. He (the speaker) was bound to say that the evidence they had hid in South Africa of the abso- lutely illimitable courage that was shown, bore testi- mony that there were just the same qualities in existence I now as there were fifty or a hundred years ago. Professor Huxley had told them that man was a fighting animal. He (Mr. Crosfield) was not one of those who endeavored to force strife, but, force he was bound to think would for a long time be the ultimate appeal. That was why they were so proud that their soldiers did their duty so well. Napoleon had told them that men felt it was easier to go into a fight in hot blood with their enemy f ice to face, than to perform the duties that their two friends had in view. It was much easier for men who bad get the fighting to do than for those who had to go ire cold blood and render assistance to wounded men, whilst bullets were raining round them. He thought therefore, that the honour due to the men who under- took that work was not in the slightest degree less than Ito those who had to go to the cannon's mouth'. (Hear, I hear.) In conclusion no said he was very pleased indeed to have had the honour of supporting what had been I said ha' their friend the Mayor. (Applause). Lieuteuane G. R. CROSbIELD amid timat Loa reason tne corps had had the honour of supplying two men I was on account of the excellent inspection I they gave to the Deputy Commissioner. He did not know whether they anew much about the number four district welch the Corps was connected with. There were at out sixty or seventy corps in it and it comprised Cheshire, Lancashire, Westmoreland, Cumberland and Ireland. Be had just heard from the Deputy Com- missioner that only sixteen men had been chosen from the district, and Warrington had two representatives. (Applause.) He had great pleasure in asking the chair- man to present the nursing certificates to Holloway and Newns. The certificates for the other successful candi- dates had not yet been signed by the President, Mr. Pierpoint who was away, and would be presented on a later occasion.

The CHAIRMAN in pregenting the certificates expressed the hope that Privates Newns and Holloway might prosper and come back safely and that he might have the honour and privilege of taking part in the hearty wel- come home that wou'd be accorded to them. (Applause.)

The Ex-Maxon 94id that with all his heart he wished " God speed" to the two volunteers. He hoped God would grant them health and strength and that they would come tack te their homes safe and well. He thought the werk they were doing was a noble work. (Applause.) The Mayor and ex-Mayor then left the room amid hearty cheers. The toasts of the visitors coupled with the names of Mr. Peter Hylande and M. A. H. Crosfield was honoured.

The CHAIRMAN repliod,and the singing of the National Anthem termin-Ald the proceedings at the hotel. At eleven o'clock a torchlight procession was formed outside the Hotel and headed by the Borough Band the processionists proceeded to the Central Station, the two volunteers being carried shoulder high through the ,itreets, and loud cheers were raised the whole distance. At the station, the proceedings were of the most enthusi- astic character. The two men left by the 11-53 train for London, and as the train steamed out of the station the band struck up "Auld Lang Syne? Cheer after cheer was raised until the train was lost to view.

div.head: Steamer Sunk in the Ship Canal.
div.p: Steamer Sunk in the Ship Canal.

The steamer Annie Hough—formerly known as the Melrose—uppn which Carey, the notorious Irish informer, was shot, was sunk in the Ship Canal on Friday. It appears that the ship,en route from Man- chester to London with a valuable general cargo, struck the canal bank with her port bow at Moore- lane, between Warrington and Runcorn, and re- ceived damage below the water-line. She com- menced to leak badly .and water rapioly gathered in the forehold. The captain determined to reach the pontoon dock at Ellesmere Port if possible. On arriving at the Port, however, the pontoon was not available, and the ship was berthed alongside Stewart's Wharf, where she sank and grounded in 201 t. of water, the water in the hold being on a level with the water in the canal. A portion of the cargo was landed on the quay side, but a large quantity is ruined by water, and the loss will be very heavy. The owners, Messrs. Samuel Hough and Companv,of Liverpool, at once took steps to re- pair the damage and raise the ship. The water- way is clear for traffic. Cheshire County Council.

The Cheshire County Council has issued pamph- lets containing reports on the experiments on potato cultivation and on testing of cattle for tuberculosis, which have been carried out by the Council. Copies may be had on application to Mr. It. P. Ward, Organising Secretary's Office, Crewe.— With regard to the tuberculin tests the report states that the number of animals tested, was 71, and of these 50 were declared free from tuberculosis, 17 were found affected, and four were dottinful. These four were afterwards found to be affected. Milk from 11 of the affected animals was microscopi- cally examined by Professor Delepine, of Owens College, Nlanchester, and in only one sample were tubercle bacilli found, and these were in a large clump. The chief conclusions deduced from the experiments are that tuberculin is a safe and reli- able test, but at present it cannot be said whether it has a curative effect, though the results so far obtained point otherwise. It is added that the number of animals aft!cted with tuberculosis is not so great as has been stated, and the percentage of those so affected which give tuberculous milk is lower than is generally represented.

WARRINGTON UNION.— ELECTION OF MEDICAL OFFICER for No. 4or NEWT ON DIS TRICT, and for No. 5 or HAYDOCK DISTRICT. NOTICE IS HEREBY GIVEN that the Guardians of the Warrington Union will on WEDNESDAY, the third day of January, 1930, proceed to the appointment of a Medical Officer for the Newton Medical District or the Union com- prising the Townships of Newton, Burtonwood and Winwick- with-Hulme, at an annual salary of £75. The population of this District is 14892 (1891 census) and the area 8040 acres or thereabouts. Upon the same day the Guardians will also proceed to the appointment ef a Medioal Officer for the No. sor Haydock District eom prising the Township of Haydock —at an annual salary of £35. The population of this District is 6535 0891 census) and the area 3103 acres or thereabouts. The Medical Officers will be required to reside in the respective districts to attend all paupers therein in case of sickness to provide all medicines (except Quinine,Cod Liver Oil,Morphia Cinchona,: lodine and balicylate of Soda,) and medical and surgical appliances and generally to perform all the duties of a District Medical Officer as prescribed by the Local Govern- ment Board General Orders. Each Medical Officer will also be appointed Public Vaccinator for his District. —The appoint- ment will be subject to the Provisions of the Poor Law Officers Superannuation Ast 1896. Candidates forthe appoint- ment must be legally qualified Medical Practitioners, registered under the Medical Act 1858 and must produce their Diplomas, Certificates or Licences to the Guardia ne. Applications and Testimonials (not more than 3) with proofs of qualification must be sent to me on or before Saturday the 30th day of December, 1899, and the candidates themselves must attend the meeting of the said Guardians on the said 3rd day of January 1900, at eleven o'clock in the Forenoon, at the Board Room at the said Warrington Union Workhouse when and where the Election will take place. Canvassing the Guardims is strictly prohibited and will be deemed a disqualification. By Order of the Board JAMES C. SUTTON, Union Clerk. Bewsey Chambers, Warrington, 7th December, 1899,
